title: Hygiene: how soap, water and clean habits keep germs away
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home with the materials listed. Changes made: the haldi test now says to score clumps of powder, not the faint yellow dye haldi leaves on skin, and to wash fully between rounds so each round starts fresh. The pepper test works only once per plate of water, so it says to use fresh water and a rinsed plate for each try. The jar test gives amounts, says the plain jar separates in 1 to 3 minutes, and says to stop at 10 minutes and write 'more than 600 seconds' if the soapy jar is still cloudy. Bar soap flakes work but slowly. The bread test says packet bread with preservatives can take 10 days or more, so bakery bread or pav is better, and that a mouldy soap slice is a real result to talk about. The bags are never opened. The reetha activity now says to soak the shells at least 15 minutes beforehand, and what to do if they have not soaked long. The tippy-tap was redesigned so it really tips: it hangs by a taped string round its middle, three-quarters full, with the foot string on its neck. The maths problem was changed to match. The Sneeze Catcher uses food colour or ink, because haldi blocks a spray nozzle. The timeline lets children write words instead of drawing all 8 cards, so it fits 25 minutes. Germ Journey has a rule for when the cards run out and a clear goal for one player: keep both germs out for 15 rolls. Make a Micelle needs 2 or more players. Parents should know: the bread test runs for a week, the haldi stains clothes and towels, reetha stings in the eyes, and the private-parts card is short and plain about body safety. The Semmelweis card and chart say honestly that mothers died; read it first and tell it calmly.

summary.text: This unit is about hygiene. Hygiene means the habits that keep our bodies, food, water and homes clean, so germs do not make us ill. Germs are tiny living things, far too small to see. They ride on our hands, in water, on food and in sneezes. Water alone slides off the oily layer where germs hold on. Soap is made of tiny two-ended molecules. One end grabs oil and the other grabs water, so soap lifts germs off and washes them away. It can even break open some viruses. About 180 years ago, doctors did not believe that their own hands carried illness. A doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis, and the midwives whose ward he compared with his own, helped show that they did. Most microbes are not germs at all. Millions of friendly ones live on your skin, and hygiene is about washing at the right moments, not killing everything. How your body fights the germs that do get in is in the unit on the immune system.
summary.art: A child's soapy hands under a running tap, with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny two-ended soap molecules wrapping a blob of oil and a germ, and friendly microbes waving from the skin around it.

intro.hook: Rub a drop of cooking oil on your palm. Now rinse it with plain water and touch a sheet of paper. Is the oil gone? Now try again with soap.
intro.text: Your hands touch hundreds of things every day: door handles, coins, your pet, your face. Tiny living things ride along on each touch. Most are harmless, and many are friends. A few can give you a tummy ache or a cold. You cannot see any of them. So how do we know they are there? And how can a little bar of soap and some water get rid of them, when water alone cannot?
intro.art: A child looking puzzled at a shiny, oily palm with water drops beading and rolling off it, a bar of soap waiting beside the tap.

outcomes: I can say what germs are, where they live, and the main ways they travel from one person to another.
I can explain how soap works: its two-ended molecules hold oil and water, lift germs off and break some viruses open.
I can wash my hands properly, for at least 20 seconds, at the moments that matter most, and test cleaning fairly.
I can say how to care for each outer part of my body, and that my private parts are mine, kept clean and private.
I can explain how clean water, toilets, covered food and no standing water keep a whole street healthy, and who does that work.
I can tell how people found out that germs cause illness, including Semmelweis, the midwives, and the scientists who came after.
I can explain that most microbes are harmless or helpful, that clean does not mean germ-free, and what scientists still do not know.

terms.meaning: The habits that keep our bodies, food, water and homes clean, so that germs do not make us ill.
terms.example: Washing your hands with soap before you eat is hygiene. So is covering a pot of water.
terms.art: A small collage: soapy hands, a covered water matka, a toothbrush and a swept doorstep.

terms.meaning: Any living thing too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria, many fungi and tiny algae are microbes.
terms.example: The microbes in curd turn milk sour and thick.
terms.art: A drop of water under a magnifier full of tiny shapes: rods, balls and spirals.

terms.meaning: A microbe, or a virus, that can make us ill. Only a small number of microbes are germs.
terms.example: The germ that causes cholera lives in dirty water.
terms.art: A crowd of friendly round microbes, with just one or two spiky germs among them.

terms.meaning: Living things made of just one tiny cell each. They live almost everywhere: in soil, water, air, and on and in you. One of them is called a bacterium.
terms.example: Bacteria in the soil turn fallen leaves back into soil.
terms.art: A zoomed-in heap of soil with rod-shaped bacteria nibbling a leaf.

terms.meaning: A tiny packet of instructions in a coat, far smaller than bacteria. It can only make copies of itself inside a living cell. Some viruses wear an oily outer coat.
terms.example: The common cold and flu are caused by viruses.
terms.art: A round virus with an oily bubble-like coat and little spikes, next to a much bigger bacterium for size.

terms.meaning: A tiny group of atoms joined together. Everything is made of molecules: water, oil, soap and you.
terms.example: One drop of water has more water molecules in it than there are stars we can see.
terms.art: A drop of water zooming into tiny V-shaped water molecules.

terms.meaning: A cleaner made of molecules with two different ends. One end loves water. The other end loves oil and grease.
terms.example: A bar of soap, liquid handwash and dishwashing liquid all work this way.
terms.art: A soap molecule drawn like a tadpole: a round head labelled water-loving and a long tail labelled oil-loving.

terms.meaning: Some molecules stick to water. Others avoid water and stick to oil. Oil and water do not mix, because water molecules hold on to each other and push oil out.
terms.example: Oil floats in a layer on top of water in a glass.
terms.art: A glass with yellow oil sitting on top of water in a neat layer.

terms.meaning: A tiny ball made by many soap molecules. Their oily tails point inwards and hold oil and dirt. Their heads face out into the water. The water carries the balls away.
terms.example: When you rinse soapy hands, millions of micelles go down the drain with the grease inside.
terms.art: A ring of tadpole-shaped soap molecules with tails pointing to a blob of oil in the middle and heads pointing out into blue water.

terms.meaning: The pull between water molecules at the top of water. It makes the surface act a little like a stretchy skin.
terms.example: A water strider insect can stand on a pond because of surface tension.
terms.art: A water strider standing on a pond, its feet making small dips in the water's surface.

terms.meaning: The idea, now proven, that many illnesses are caused by germs passing from one place or person to another.
terms.example: Germ theory is why doctors wash their hands and boil their tools.
terms.art: A doctor washing hands in a basin beside a microscope with a germ on its slide.

terms.meaning: A person, usually a woman, trained to help mothers give birth and to care for new babies.
terms.example: In many Indian villages, a trained midwife or nurse helps when a baby is born.
terms.art: A smiling midwife holding a newborn baby wrapped in a soft cloth.

terms.meaning: All the microbes that live together in one place, such as your skin, your gut or a patch of soil.
terms.example: Your skin's microbiome is different on your elbow and on your forehead.
terms.art: A hand drawn like a map, with different neighbourhoods of microbes on the palm, fingers and back.

terms.meaning: Resident microbes live on your skin all the time. Visitor microbes are picked up from things you touch. Washing removes mostly the visitors.
terms.example: After you pat a street dog, its microbes are visitors on your hand.
terms.art: A hand with small home-like microbes settled in the skin, and suitcase-carrying visitor microbes on top being washed away.

terms.meaning: A natural soap-like molecule made by some plants. Like soap, it has a water-loving end and an oil-loving end.
terms.example: Reetha, the soapnut, makes foam in water because it is full of saponins.
terms.art: Brown wrinkly reetha shells in a bowl of water with white foam on top.

terms.meaning: Reetha is the dried fruit of the soapnut tree. Shikakai is the pod of a climbing acacia plant. People in India have washed hair and clothes with them for centuries.
terms.example: Many grandmothers still soak reetha and shikakai to wash hair.
terms.art: A bowl of dried reetha fruits and a pile of brown shikakai pods on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: To kill most of the germs on something, using heat or a strong chemical.
terms.example: Boiling drinking water for one minute kills the germs in it.
terms.art: A steel pot of water boiling on a stove with bubbles rising.

terms.meaning: Keeping a place clean and healthy with toilets, drains, safe water and taking rubbish away.
terms.example: A clean public toilet and a covered drain are sanitation.
terms.art: A tidy street with a covered drain, a clean public toilet and a worker in gloves sweeping.

terms.meaning: The soft, wet linings of your eyes, nose and mouth. Germs get into the body most easily here.
terms.example: That is why we wash hands before rubbing our eyes or eating.
terms.art: A child's face with the eyes, nose and mouth gently highlighted as soft, wet doorways.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what caused the difference.
terms.example: To test soap against water, use the same pretend germs, the same time and the same hands.
terms.art: Two identical hands side by side, one under plain water and one with soap, a timer between them.

explanations.concept: What germs are, and how they travel
explanations.definition: Germs are microbes or viruses that can make us ill. They travel on hands, in water and food, through the air in sneezes and coughs, and on insects like flies and mosquitoes.
explanations.description: Germs cannot walk or fly by themselves. They get carried. Most of the time, hands carry them. A hand touches a dirty surface, then touches the eyes, nose or mouth. Those soft, wet linings are the easiest way into the body. A sneeze sprays tiny drops that carry germs across a room. Dirty water and uncovered food carry germs into the tummy. Flies land on rubbish and then on food. Mosquitoes carry malaria and dengue germs from one person to the next. So hygiene is really about breaking the chain at each step. How the body fights germs that get past its walls is in the unit on the immune system.
examples: A child plays with a ball outside, then eats a samosa without washing. Germs ride from the ball, to the hand, to the mouth.
A sneeze into the air can spray drops more than a metre. A sneeze into your elbow keeps most of them on your sleeve.
A fly on an open rubbish heap can carry germs on its feet to uncovered food.
explanations.art: A chain of pictures joined by arrows: a dirty ball, a hand, a samosa, a mouth, with a big soap bar breaking the chain between hand and samosa.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea behind hygiene: germs are carried from place to place, and we can break the chain.

explanations.concept: Why water alone is not enough
explanations.definition: Skin is covered in a thin layer of natural oil. Many germs and much dirt stick in that oil. Water slides off oil, so water alone leaves most of them behind.
explanations.description: Your skin makes its own oil, called sebum. It keeps skin soft and waterproof. It also makes a sticky layer where dirt and germs hold on. Water molecules hold tightly on to each other. They do not hold on to oil. So when you rinse an oily hand, the water runs over the oil and away, leaving the oil and its germs behind. You saw this if you rubbed oil on your palm and rinsed it. Rubbing hard under water does help a little, because rubbing knocks some things loose. But to really lift oil, you need something that can hold oil and water at the same time.
examples: An oily steel plate rinsed with plain water still feels greasy.
Drops of water bead up and roll off an oily hand instead of spreading.
explanations.art: A close-up of skin with a thin shiny oil layer, germs stuck in it, and water drops rolling over the top without picking them up.
explanations.context: Have you noticed an oily plate stays greasy under plain water? This card explains why water alone cannot clean off oily dirt and germs.

explanations.concept: How soap works, down to the molecules
explanations.definition: A soap molecule has a head that loves water and a long tail that loves oil. The tails dig into oily dirt and germs. The heads face the water. Many soap molecules surround the oil in tiny balls called micelles, and the water carries them away.
explanations.description: Picture a soap molecule like a tiny tadpole. Its round head sticks to water. Its long tail hates water and hides in oil. When you rub soap on oily hands, millions of tails push into the oil. They pry little blobs of oil off your skin. The tails stay inside each blob and the heads point outwards. Now each blob is wrapped in heads that love water. So water can grab the blob and wash it down the drain, with the germs inside. The rubbing helps a lot, because it breaks the oil into small pieces. That is why we rub for at least 20 seconds. Soap also does something to some viruses. Flu viruses and coronaviruses wear an oily outer coat. Soap tails push into that coat and break it apart, so the virus falls to pieces.
examples: Dishwashing liquid lifts oil off a kadhai the same way that handwash lifts it off your hands.
In the oil, water and soap jar test, soap turns the clear layers into one cloudy mix. The cloudiness is millions of tiny micelles.
explanations.art: A four-step zoom: soapy hands; a blob of oil on skin; tadpole-shaped soap molecules pushing their tails into it; a finished ball of soap molecules floating away in water with the oil and a germ inside.
explanations.context: This card zooms right in, past anything a microscope can show, to explain how a bar of soap really cleans your hands.

explanations.concept: Soap's molecules are built like your own cell walls
explanations.definition: Every cell in your body is wrapped in a thin skin made of molecules with water-loving heads and oil-loving tails, just like soap. The oily coat of some viruses is made the same way. That is why soap can break it.
explanations.description: Each of your cells has a wall around it called a membrane. It is made of two layers of molecules. Their water-loving heads face out, towards the watery outside and the watery inside. Their oil-loving tails tuck into the middle, away from water. The oily coat of a flu virus is built the same way, from the cell the virus came from. Soap molecules are similar enough to slip in and pull the coat apart. Your own skin is safe, because its top layer is made of tough, dead cells. Some scientists think the very first cells, billions of years ago, began when molecules like these folded into tiny bubbles in water. That is still an idea, being tested in laboratories.
examples: A soap bubble is a thin film of water held between two layers of soap molecules.
Washing with soap too often can dry out skin, because soap also lifts some of the skin's own oil.
explanations.art: Side by side: a soap bubble's film, a cell membrane and a virus coat, each drawn as rows of tadpole molecules, heads out and tails in.
explanations.context: This card shows a surprise: the molecule in a bar of soap is built like the walls of your own cells.

explanations.concept: When and how to wash your hands
explanations.definition: Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, rubbing every part, at the moments germs are most likely to travel.
explanations.description: The most important moments are before you eat or touch food, after using the toilet, after blowing your nose or sneezing, after playing outside or with animals, and when you come home. Wet your hands. Add soap. Rub palms, then the backs of your hands, between your fingers, round each thumb, your fingertips and nails, and your wrists. Twenty seconds is about the time it takes to sing Happy Birthday twice. Rinse well. Then dry your hands on a clean towel or let them dry in the air. Wet hands pass on germs more easily than dry ones. Warm water and cold water work about the same. Plain soap works about as well as soap that says antibacterial, for everyday washing.
examples: In the haldi test, the yellow stayed longest between fingers, round the thumbs and under nails.
A study found that washing hands with soap can cut tummy illnesses like diarrhoea by about a third, or more.
explanations.art: Six small pictures of hands in order: palms rubbing, backs, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips on palm, wrists, with a little clock showing 20 seconds.
explanations.context: This card gives the steps for washing hands well, and the moments when washing matters most.

explanations.concept: Caring for the outside of your body
explanations.definition: Each outer part of the body has its own way of staying healthy. Hygiene helps the body do what it is already doing.
explanations.description: Bathe every day, or at least often, to wash away sweat, dead skin and visitor germs. Brush your teeth twice a day, morning and night, so mouth bacteria cannot turn sugar into acid that makes holes. Keep nails short and clean, because dirt and germs hide under them. Wash and comb hair, and check for lice, tiny insects that anyone can get. Never poke anything inside your ears. Earwax cleans itself out. Do not rub your eyes with dirty hands. Blow your nose into a hanky or tissue, then wash your hands. Wear chappals outside, because some worm larvae in dirty soil can get in through bare feet. Your private parts, the parts covered by underwear, are kept clean and private. Your body belongs to you. If any touch feels wrong, say no, get away, and tell a grown-up you trust.
examples: A neem datun, a chewed twig, was India's toothbrush for centuries. Today dentists add fluoride toothpaste, which protects teeth from acid.
Hookworm larvae in soil can enter through the skin of bare feet. Chappals stop them.
explanations.art: A friendly outline of a child with small labels and pictures: a toothbrush at the mouth, short clean nails, a comb in the hair, chappals on the feet, a hanky near the nose.
explanations.context: This card goes round the outside of the body, one part at a time, with a plain way to care for each.

explanations.concept: Clean surroundings keep a whole street healthy
explanations.definition: Safe water, toilets, covered drains, covered food, rubbish taken away and no standing water stop germs from spreading to many people at once.
explanations.description: One family washing their hands helps that family. Clean water and toilets help a whole town. Germs from human waste can get into water and food, and make many people ill at once. That is why toilets and clean drains matter so much. Boiling or filtering drinking water kills or removes most germs. Covered food keeps flies off. Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water, even a little water in a flowerpot tray or a coconut shell. The eggs become flying mosquitoes in about a week in warm weather. So emptying every container of still water once a week stops them. In 2014, India began the Swachh Bharat Mission to build toilets and clean streets. Sanitation workers, many of whom do hard and risky work for little thanks, keep towns healthy every day.
examples: A cooler or a tyre left with water in it can grow hundreds of mosquitoes in a week.
ASHA workers, women health workers in Indian villages, visit families to talk about clean water, toilets and mosquitoes.
explanations.art: A cheerful Indian lane: a covered water tank, a flowerpot tray tipped out, a covered drain, a woman health worker talking to a family at their door.
explanations.context: This card goes beyond one person's hands. It shows how a clean street, clean water and toilets keep everyone healthy.

explanations.concept: How we found out about germs
explanations.definition: Germ theory says that many illnesses are caused by tiny living things passed from one person or place to another. It took hundreds of years and many people to show this.
explanations.description: Long ago, many people thought illness came from bad smells in the air, or from bad luck. Some guessed the truth early. In 1546, an Italian doctor, Girolamo Fracastoro, wrote that diseases might spread by tiny invisible seeds. In the 1670s, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth-seller in the Netherlands, made his own tiny lenses. He saw 'little animals' swimming in pond water and in the white stuff scraped off his teeth. Nobody yet linked them to illness. In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that doctors' unwashed hands were carrying illness to mothers. In 1854, Filippo Pacini in Italy saw the cholera germ, and John Snow in London showed that cholera spread through one water pump. In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur showed that microbes come from other microbes, not from nowhere. Joseph Lister began cleaning wounds and tools in surgery in 1867. In 1884, Robert Koch, working in Kolkata and in Egypt, grew the cholera germ and convinced the world.
examples: Pacini described the cholera germ in 1854, thirty years before Koch. Hardly anyone noticed. Today the germ's full name includes his name: Vibrio cholerae Pacini 1854.
Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole cared for soldiers in the 1850s. Nightingale used careful counts to show that clean hospitals saved lives.
explanations.art: A timeline along a washing line, with pegged pictures: a tiny lens, a hand-washing basin, a water pump with its handle removed, a swan-necked glass flask and a microscope.
explanations.context: We now know germs cause many illnesses. This card tells how people found out, step by step, over about 350 years.

explanations.concept: Semmelweis, the midwives and the washing basin
explanations.definition: In 1847 in Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that mothers in the doctors' ward fell ill because doctors carried something from dead bodies on their hands. Washing hands in chlorine water made the illness drop sharply.
explanations.description: Vienna's big hospital had two wards for mothers having babies. In one, doctors and students helped the mothers. In the other, midwives did. Many more mothers caught a dangerous fever, called childbed fever, in the doctors' ward. The midwives' ward was much safer. Mothers knew this and begged to go there. Semmelweis wanted to know why. The doctors often came straight from cutting open dead bodies to learn anatomy. The midwives never did. Then his friend, Jakob Kolletschka, was cut by a student's knife during that work. He fell ill with the same fever, and died. Semmelweis guessed that something from the dead bodies was being carried on hands. Soap did not even remove the smell. So he made everyone wash in chlorine water, which did. In April 1847, about 18 out of every 100 mothers in the doctors' ward died. After washing began in May, it fell to about 2 out of every 100 by the summer.
examples: The midwives' ward was the clue. Without their safer ward to compare with, nobody would have known the doctors' ward could be safer.
Many doctors were offended at the idea that their own hands caused illness. Semmelweis lost his job in Vienna and died in 1865, before most doctors accepted his idea.
explanations.art: A long hospital ward in 1847 with a basin of water by the door, a young doctor washing his hands, and a midwife in an apron looking on.
explanations.context: This card tells the story of one of the most important hand-washes in history, in a hospital in Vienna about 180 years ago.

chart.title: Mothers who died of childbed fever in the doctors' ward, out of every 100
chart.note: Hand-washing with chlorine water began in the middle of May 1847. These are the real numbers Semmelweis wrote down, rounded.

show.art: A doctor in an 1840s coat walking from a dissecting room straight to a mother's bed, without washing.
show.caption: Before May 1847: doctors went straight from dead bodies to mothers.

show.art: The same doctor washing his hands in a basin of chlorine water by the ward door.
show.caption: From May 1847: everyone washed in chlorine water first.

explanations.concept: Most microbes are friends, not germs
explanations.definition: Only a small number of the world's microbes cause illness. Most are harmless, and many are needed: on our skin, in our gut, in soil, in food and in the sea.
explanations.description: Your skin is home to millions of microbes. Some kinds of them make substances that stop harmful bacteria from growing. Washing with soap removes mostly the visitors, the microbes picked up from things you touch. Most residents live deeper in the skin's folds and pores, and stay. Microbes in your gut help digest food. Microbes turn milk into curd and make idli and dosa batter rise. Soil microbes turn dead leaves into new soil. Tiny ocean microbes make a large share of the oxygen in the air. Microbes also matter for themselves, not just for what they do for us. They were here for billions of years before any animal. The unit on the immune system tells how your friendly microbes help guard you.
examples: Leave a little curd in warm milk overnight, and its microbes turn the milk into new curd.
Cows can live on grass only because microbes in their stomachs break the grass down.
explanations.art: A busy, friendly scene: a curd pot, an idli steamer, a pile of leaves turning to soil and a green sea, each with smiling microbes at work.
explanations.context: Germs get all the attention. This card is about the far bigger number of microbes that are harmless or helpful.

explanations.description: Hygiene saves millions of lives. But some scientists noticed something puzzling. Allergies, such as hay fever and some kinds of asthma, became more common as homes got cleaner. Could living with too few microbes be part of the reason? Scientists still argue about this.
examples: Children who grow up on farms with animals tend to have fewer allergies.
No study has shown that washing hands before meals causes allergies.

perspectives.who: David Strachan, a British doctor, in 1989
perspectives.explanation: He studied over 17,000 British children. Those with more older brothers and sisters had less hay fever. He suggested that catching more infections when very young might protect against allergies. This became known as the hygiene hypothesis.

perspectives.who: Graham Rook, a British scientist, in 2003, and many scientists today
perspectives.explanation: It is not catching illnesses that helps. It is meeting the harmless 'old friends' microbes that people lived with for thousands of years, in soil, plants, animals and other people.

perspectives.who: Sally Bloomfield, a British hygiene scientist, and others
perspectives.explanation: Calling it a hygiene problem is misleading, because it makes people stop washing hands. She argues for targeted hygiene: wash well at the key moments, such as before food and after the toilet, and otherwise let children play outside, in mud and with animals.

explanations.art: A child happily digging in a garden with muddy hands, then washing them with soap before eating a roti, with a question mark between the two pictures.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument among scientists: can a home be too clean?

explanations.definition: Some plants make their own soap-like molecules, called saponins. Reetha and shikakai are full of them, which is why they foam and clean.
explanations.description: The soapnut tree's fruit, reetha, makes a rich foam when rubbed in water. Its saponins have a water-loving part and an oil-loving part, just like soap. People in India have used reetha and shikakai to wash hair, silk and jewellery for centuries. Soap as we know it is made by mixing fat or oil with a strong alkali, a chemical that came long ago from wood ash. Some of the oldest known recipes for soap-like cleaners, mixing fat and ash, come from Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, over 4,000 years ago. Plants probably make saponins to protect themselves from insects and fungi, not for us.
examples: Soak a few reetha shells in warm water and squeeze them. White foam appears.
Ash was used to scrub steel and brass pots in many Indian homes, because it is alkaline and cuts grease.
explanations.art: A soapnut tree heavy with round fruits, and below it a bowl of reetha foam beside a modern bar of soap.
explanations.context: Long before soap bars, people cleaned with plants. This card explains why plants like reetha can clean.

explanations.definition: Many animals keep themselves and their homes clean in their own ways, which helps keep away germs and pests.
explanations.description: Cats lick their fur clean with rough tongues. Birds preen, combing their feathers with their beaks and spreading oil from a gland near the tail. Elephants and sparrows take dust baths that help keep away insects. Monkeys groom each other, picking out dirt and insects. Grooming is also how they show friendship. In the sea, little cleaner fish set up 'cleaning stations', and big fish wait their turn to have tiny pests picked off. In a beehive, some bees are cleaners. They clean out the wax cells and carry dead bees out of the hive, so illness does not spread.
examples: A crow splashing in a puddle on a hot afternoon is bathing.
Monkeys sitting in pairs on a temple wall, one combing the other's fur, are grooming.
explanations.art: A cat licking its paw, a crow splashing in a puddle, an elephant tossing dust, and two monkeys grooming on a wall.
explanations.context: People are not the only ones who keep clean. This card looks at how other animals do it, for their own reasons.

explanations.description: In 1896, a British scientist working in India, Ernest Hanbury Hankin, tested water from the Ganga and the Yamuna. Something in the river water killed cholera germs in his tests, and it passed through a fine filter. Twenty years later, scientists found viruses that attack only bacteria. They are called bacteriophages, which means bacteria-eaters. Many scientists think Hankin was seeing bacteriophages at work. Nobody can be sure today, because his water samples are long gone. Doctors are now testing bacteriophages as medicines for germs that antibiotics can no longer kill.
examples: Bacteriophages are the most common living-like things on Earth. There are more of them in the sea than stars in the universe.
A bacteriophage looks a little like a tiny moon-lander, landing on a bacterium.

perspectives.explanation: Hankin's result was very likely caused by bacteriophages in the river water.
We cannot check his water now, and other things in the water may have played a part. River water today is not safe to drink without boiling.

explanations.art: A zoomed-in drop of river water where tiny lander-shaped bacteriophages settle on a rod-shaped cholera bacterium.
explanations.context: This card is about a puzzle from India, 130 years ago, that led to viruses which hunt germs.

agreed.text: Many illnesses are caused by germs that pass from person to person, or through water, food, air and insects.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can grow germs, see them under microscopes, read their genes and follow how they spread. Stopping their path stops the illness, as John Snow showed with a water pump in 1854.

agreed.text: Washing hands with soap and water removes most germs and dirt from hands.
agreed.evidence: Many tests count germs on hands before and after washing. Studies in homes, schools and villages show fewer tummy illnesses and colds where people wash with soap.

agreed.text: Soap works because its molecules hold both oil and water.
agreed.evidence: Chemists know the shape of soap molecules. The oil, water and soap jar test shows soap mixing oil into water.

agreed.text: Safe water and toilets are some of the best protections against illness ever invented.
agreed.evidence: In many countries, illnesses like cholera fell sharply after clean water pipes and sewers were built, often before medicines for them existed.

agreed.text: Most microbes are harmless or helpful, and our bodies carry many friendly ones.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have read the genes of the microbes on skin and in the gut. They find thousands of kinds, most of them living peacefully with us.

challenging.claim: Illness is caused by bad smells in the air, called miasma.
challenging.who: Many doctors and thinkers for over 2,000 years, in Europe, India and China
challenging.for: Dirty, smelly places really did have more illness. Cleaning them up helped.
challenging.against: The smell was not the cause. The germs in the dirt and water were. John Snow showed that cholera followed one water pump, not the bad air. Germs were later seen and grown in laboratories.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where illness comes from.

challenging.claim: Ignaz Semmelweis alone discovered why hand-washing saves lives.
challenging.for: He collected the numbers and made the doctors wash. That was brave and new.
challenging.against: His clue came from comparing his ward with the midwives' ward, where far fewer mothers fell ill. The midwives' skill made that comparison possible. Others had suspected it too. In 1843, Oliver Wendell Holmes in America wrote that doctors could carry childbed fever. And in Scotland, in 1795, Alexander Gordon had said the same.
challenging.context: This card asks who should get credit for discovering that hand-washing saves mothers' lives.

challenging.claim: All bacteria are bad, and we should kill as many as we can.
challenging.who: A common belief, helped by adverts for cleaning products
challenging.for: Some bacteria cause serious illness, and killing them saves lives.
challenging.against: Most bacteria are harmless or helpful. Our skin and gut need them. Killing them everywhere would harm us and the soil, sea and air. Soap mostly lifts germs off hands, which is what we need.
challenging.context: This card looks at a common idea about bacteria, and whether it is true.

challenging.claim: Antibacterial soap is much better than ordinary soap.
challenging.for: It contains chemicals that kill some bacteria.
challenging.against: For everyday hand-washing at home, tests found it no better than plain soap and water. In 2016, the United States food and medicine authority stopped some of these chemicals being sold in home soaps for this reason. Some scientists also worry they may help germs become resistant.
challenging.context: This card is about whether you need special antibacterial soap at home.

challenging.claim: Hot water kills germs on your hands, so it must be hot to work.
challenging.for: Very hot water, like boiling water, does kill germs.
challenging.against: Water hot enough to kill germs would burn your skin. In a 2017 study in America, warm and cold water removed germs about equally well. The soap and the rubbing do the work.
challenging.context: This card asks whether the water for hand-washing needs to be hot.

challenging.claim: Children today are ill with allergies because homes are too clean.
challenging.who: A popular version of the hygiene hypothesis
challenging.for: Allergies rose as homes got cleaner. Farm children with animals have fewer allergies.
challenging.against: Washing hands and cleaning kitchens has not been shown to cause allergies. Many scientists now think the real change is less time outdoors, fewer animals, and less contact with harmless soil microbes.
challenging.context: This card looks at a popular idea about clean homes and allergies.

big_questions.q: If you cannot see germs, how can you know they are there?
big_questions.hint: Think of the mould on the bread slices, and of how Semmelweis used numbers.

big_questions.q: Why does a molecule with two different ends clean better than one that loves only water?
big_questions.hint: Think about what water does with oil, and what soap does with both.

big_questions.q: Millions of microbes live on your skin. Are they part of you, or guests?
big_questions.hint: Your skin is their home. Would your skin be healthy without them?

big_questions.q: Doctors were offended when Semmelweis said their hands carried illness. Why is it so hard to accept that you might be causing harm?
big_questions.hint: Think of a time you found out you were wrong. How did it feel?

big_questions.q: Is anything truly dirty? Or is dirt just something in the wrong place?
big_questions.hint: Soil is lovely in a garden. Is it lovely on your dinner plate?

big_questions.q: One family washing hands helps one family. Who keeps a whole town clean, and do they get enough thanks?
big_questions.hint: Think of the people who sweep streets and clean drains near your home.

big_questions.q: Plants like reetha made soap molecules long before people did. Why might a plant need soap?
big_questions.hint: Think of insects and fungi that might want to eat the fruit.

big_questions.q: Your cell walls are built like soap. Why doesn't soap wash your own cells away?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tough, dead top layer of your skin.

big_questions.q: If microbes were here billions of years before any animal, whose world is it really?
big_questions.hint: Who was here first? Who could live without whom?

big_questions.q: Can a place be too clean for living things?
big_questions.hint: Think of farm children and allergies, and of the microbes in soil.

story.title: The Basin by the Door
story.note: Real: the Vienna General Hospital, its two maternity wards (doctors and students in one, midwives in the other), the mothers begging to go to the midwives' ward, Jakob Kolletschka's death in March 1847, Semmelweis choosing chlorine water because ordinary soap did not remove the smell from his hands, the basin at the door from May 1847, and the fall in deaths. Imagined: Anna, her mother Liesl, the midwife Frau Weber, the laundry's chlorine water as the hint, and everything they say.
text: My mother washed the sheets of the Vienna General Hospital, and I helped her. In the year 1847 I was nine years old. I carried the baskets. I knew every corridor by its smell. The kitchen smelled of cabbage. The chapel smelled of candles. And the long room where the student doctors cut open the bodies of the dead, to learn how people are made, smelled of something sweet and wrong that stayed in your nose all day.

There were two wards for mothers having babies. The First Ward belonged to the doctors and their students. The Second Ward belonged to the midwives. They were next to each other. They had the same beds, the same soup and the same grey windows. My mother washed their sheets in the same tubs, with the same soap.

But the mothers knew something. On the days the First Ward took new mothers, women cried at the gate. Some begged on their knees to be taken to the Second Ward instead. 'In the First Ward,' one whispered to me, 'the fever comes.' It was called childbed fever. In the First Ward, many mothers caught it after their babies were born, and some of them did not get better. In the midwives' ward, it came much less often.
'Why?' I asked my mother. 'It is the same building.'
'If I knew that,' said my mother, scrubbing hard, 'I would be a professor and not a washerwoman.'

I asked Frau Weber, the oldest midwife, who smelled of lavender and gave me plums. She was quiet for a while. 'We count everything here,' she said. 'Every mother, every baby, every fever. The numbers do not lie. Our ward is safer. Nobody upstairs has asked us why.'

Somebody upstairs did ask, in the end. His name was Doctor Semmelweis. He was young and round-faced and always in a hurry. He asked everyone questions. He asked the midwives how they held the babies. He asked the priest which way he walked through the wards. He even asked my mother whether the First Ward's sheets were dirtier. They were not. He wrote every answer in a little book.

In March, a kind old professor, Doctor Kolletschka, died. A student's knife had slipped and nicked his finger while they worked on a body. Afterwards he fell ill with a fever, and it looked exactly like the mothers' fever. Doctor Semmelweis walked the corridors that week with a face like a closed door.

One morning he came down to the laundry. I was folding pillowcases. He stood at our big sink and washed his hands with our yellow soap, hard, for a long time. Then he held them out to me, wet and red.
'You have a good nose, child,' he said. 'Everybody says so. Smell.'
I smelled. Under the soap was the sweet, wrong smell of the cutting room. It had not gone.
'Yes,' he said quietly, as if I had told him something terrible and wonderful. 'Soap does not take it off. So something stays on our hands. Something we cannot see.'

I thought about the sheets. When a sheet came from the sick room smelling bad, ordinary soap did not fix it either. So my mother dipped it in the chlorine water, the sharp, stinging bath that bleached things white. Afterwards the sheet smelled of nothing at all.
I did not want to say it. I was nine, and he was a doctor. But I thought of Frau Weber saying that nobody upstairs ever asked. So I pointed to the chlorine tub.
He looked at it for a long moment. Then he plunged his hands in, up to the wrists, and hissed at the sting. He pulled them out and held them to my face.
I smelled. Nothing. Only the chlorine, clean and sharp.

In May, a white basin of chlorine water appeared by the door of the First Ward. Every doctor and every student had to wash in it before they touched a mother. The students grumbled. Their hands cracked and stung. One of the older doctors said it was an insult. But Doctor Semmelweis stood by the basin like a soldier, and nobody got past.

In April, I had seen many coffins leave the First Ward. In June, I saw few. In July, fewer still. Frau Weber showed me the numbers in the big book, and ran her finger down them. 'Now,' she said, 'upstairs is as safe as downstairs.' She did not smile, but she gave me two plums instead of one.

Many doctors never believed him. They said a gentleman's hands could not carry illness. It was twenty years before scientists with microscopes found the tiny living things he had guessed at. Nobody wrote down my name, or my mother's, or Frau Weber's. But I still wash my hands slowly, every time, and I still smell them afterwards. Something we cannot see is always there, until the water carries it away.
story.epiphany: For the parent: nobody in the story can see germs. The clue is a smell that soap cannot remove, so something invisible must still be on the doctors' hands. The midwives' careful counting gives the comparison, and the change of just one thing, washing in chlorine water at the door, changes the numbers. That is a fair test, and it is how the invisible was found. The story also asks quietly who gets listened to: mothers, midwives, washerwomen and a child all knew part of the answer.
ask: Why did the mothers beg to go to the midwives' ward?
The doctor's hands still smelled after soap. What did that tell him?
What changed in the First Ward in May, and what happened to the numbers?
Frau Weber said nobody upstairs ever asked the midwives. Why do you think that was?
Anna nearly did not speak. What helped her decide to point at the tub?

printables.title: 24 hygiene cards to cut out (draw one when you land on a ★)
items: Hands washed with soap for 20 seconds. Go back to START.
Hands rinsed with water only for 2 seconds. You are still stuck in the oil. Move ahead 1.
Nobody washed before eating. Move ahead 3.
Someone rubbed their eyes. Jump ahead 2.
A sneeze into the air! Move ahead 2.
A sneeze into an elbow. Miss a turn.
Food left uncovered, and a fly landed. Move ahead 2.
Food kept covered. Miss a turn.
Wet hands wiped on a dirty cloth. Move ahead 2.
Hands dried on a clean towel. Go back 3.
Nails long and dirty. You hide underneath. Move ahead 2.
Nails short and clean. Go back 2.
Drinking water boiled. Go back 4.
Water from an open, dirty tank. Move ahead 3.
Washed only the palms, not between the fingers. You hide between the fingers. Stay where you are.
Washed everywhere, even the thumbs and wrists. Go back to START.

TEST IT: rub your palms and fingers with soap for 20 seconds. Count out loud. Did it feel long?
TEST IT: touch your face as few times as you can until your next turn. Did you manage?

printables.title: Germ tokens: small paper circles with a germ drawn on each, one colour per player

rules: Each player is a germ. Put your germ token on START. You also need one dice.
Take turns. Roll the dice and move your germ that many squares along the path.
If you land on a ★ square, take the top hygiene card and do what it says.
TEST IT cards: everyone does the test together. Then the player who drew it moves ahead 1.
The first germ to reach the tummy wins the race. Then everyone talks about which cards stopped germs the most.
If the pile of cards runs out, shuffle the used cards and start a new pile.

Playing alone: move two germs, a red one and a blue one, taking turns. Your goal is to stop both germs reaching the tummy within 15 rolls, counting both germs' rolls together. Before you start, pick out 3 hygiene cards you choose to keep in your hand. You may play one instead of rolling, whenever a germ gets close.

flow.do: 1. Print or draw the 20-square path. 2. Cut out the 24 hygiene cards and shuffle them face down. 3. Give each player a germ token. 4. Have one dice ready.
flow.say: In this game, you are a germ. Germs cannot walk. They ride on hands, food and water. Your job is to ride all the way from a dirty hand to someone's tummy.
flow.kid: In this game, you are a germ! You start on a dirty hand. Try to ride all the way to a tummy.
flow.context: This is the first step of Germ Journey. It is a board game where each player is a germ trying to travel from a dirty hand into someone's tummy. Here you set it up.

flow.do: Play one practice turn together. Draw the card 'Hands rinsed with water only for 2 seconds'.
flow.say: Here is a practice card. Hands were rinsed with water only. The germ moves ahead. Why didn't the water wash it off?
flow.kid: Practice card: hands rinsed with water only. The germ moves ahead! Why did water not wash it off?

check.q: Why does a quick rinse with water only leave most germs behind?
options: Germs stick in the skin's oil, and water slides off oil
Water feeds the germs and makes them grow
Germs can swim away from the water
check.why: Skin has a thin natural oil. Many germs stick in it. Water does not hold on to oil, so it runs over the top. Soap holds oil and water both, so it lifts the germs off. Picking 'water feeds them' usually means mixing up washing with leaving things damp. Picking 'swim away' misses that the germs are stuck in the oil.

flow.do: 1. Take turns rolling and moving. 2. On a ★ square, read the card aloud and follow it. 3. When a TEST IT card comes, everyone does it.
flow.say: When you draw a card, tell us why it helps the germ or stops it.
flow.kid: Roll and move. Landed on a star? Take a card. Say why it helps or stops your germ.
flow.parent: Good reasons: soap lifts germs out of the oil, a clean towel dries without adding germs, short nails leave nowhere to hide, boiling kills germs in water, covered food keeps flies off. In the alone version, the child usually finds that the soap and boiling cards stop germs best. That is a real lesson about where to break the chain.

flow.do: When a germ reaches the tummy, stop. Sort all the cards that were drawn into two piles: helped the germ, stopped the germ.
flow.say: Which card would you most like to see at every tap in the world?
flow.kid: Sort the cards. Which helped germs? Which stopped them? Which card is the best germ-stopper?
flow.think: Germs cannot move by themselves. So who decides where they go?

games.context: This is a board game about how germs travel. Each player is a germ riding from a dirty hand towards a tummy. Hygiene cards push the germs back.

games.title: Make a Micelle

printables.title: Two big signs to put on the floor
items: DRAIN
SKIN

printables.title: 10 'oil blobs': crumpled balls of yellow paper, each with a small germ drawn on it

rules: Each player is a soap molecule. Your left hand is your oil-loving tail. Your right hand is your water-loving head.
Put the SKIN sign at one side of the room and the DRAIN sign at the other. Scatter the 10 oil blobs on the SKIN side.
Oil blobs may only be touched by tails, your left hands. Heads, your right hands, must stay pointing outwards, into the 'water'.
Work in pairs or threes. Hold one blob between your left hands, heads facing out, and walk it to the DRAIN. That is a micelle.
If the blob drops, it sticks back on the SKIN. Take it back and try again.
Clear all 10 blobs before a grown-up counts slowly to 120. Then try with only 60.

flow.do: 1. Crumple 10 sheets of scrap paper into balls, and draw a germ on each. These are the oil blobs. 2. Put the SKIN sign on one side of the room and the DRAIN on the other. 3. Scatter the blobs near SKIN. 4. Show everyone which hand is the tail and which is the head.
flow.say: You are soap molecules. Your left hand loves oil. Your right hand loves water. The yellow balls are blobs of oil, with germs stuck inside.
flow.kid: You are a soap molecule! Your left hand loves oil. Your right hand loves water. The yellow balls are oily germs.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make a Micelle. It is a moving game where players act as soap molecules carrying oil and germs off the skin and down the drain.

flow.do: 1. Players pair up. 2. They pick up a blob between their left hands only, right hands pointing outwards. 3. They carry it to DRAIN without dropping it. 4. Count slowly to 120 while they clear all 10.
flow.say: Tails hold the oil. Heads face the water. Go!
flow.kid: Hold a blob between your left hands. Keep right hands pointing out. Carry it to the drain!

ask.q: Why must the right hands point outwards?
good: The water grabs the heads and carries the ball away.

flow.parent: With two players, the parent and child are one micelle. With more players, a group of three or four around one blob looks most like a real micelle. Soft paper balls are safe to drop.

flow.do: Talk about how the game is like real soap, and how it is different.
flow.say: Real micelles are made of many soap molecules, and they are far too small to see. The rubbing of your hands breaks the oil into tiny blobs, so the soap can wrap them.
flow.kid: Real micelles are made of many soap molecules. They are far too small to see.

check.q: In a real micelle, where do the oil-loving tails of the soap molecules point?
options: Inwards, into the oil
Outwards, into the water
Every which way
check.why: The tails avoid water and stick into the oil, so they point inwards. The water-loving heads face out, so water can carry the whole ball away. Picking 'outwards' usually means mixing up the two ends. Remember: tails in the oil, heads in the water.

games.context: This is a moving game. Players are soap molecules. They must carry oily germs from the skin to the drain, holding them only with their 'oil-loving' hands.

items.p: What is a germ?
opts: A tiny living thing, or a virus, that can make us ill
items.why: A germ is a microbe or virus that can make us ill. Picking 'every microbe' is a common mix-up. Most microbes are harmless or helpful. Picking 'insect' mixes up germs with bigger pests like lice. Insects can carry germs, but they are not germs.

items.p: What is the most common way germs get into our bodies?
opts: From our hands, when we touch our eyes, nose or mouth
items.why: Hands carry germs to the eyes, nose and mouth, whose soft, wet linings let germs in easily. Picking 'clean, dry skin' usually means not knowing that skin is a strong wall. Germs need a way in, like a cut or a wet lining.

items.p: To wash your hands well, rub them with soap for at least ____ seconds.
items.why: About 20 seconds gives soap time to break up the oil on every part of your hands. That is about the time it takes to sing Happy Birthday twice.

items.p: Rinsing with water alone removes as much dirt and germs as washing with soap.
items.why: False. Germs stick in the skin's oil. Water slides off oil. Soap holds oil and water both, so it lifts the germs away. The haldi test shows this.

items.p: Sort these moments. Should you wash your hands with soap now?
cats: No need to wash just for this
items: before eating lunch
Wash now
after using the toilet
Wash now
after reading a book in bed
No need to wash just for this
after playing with a dog
Wash now
after blowing your nose
Wash now
after singing a song
No need to wash just for this
items.why: Wash at the moments germs travel most: before food, after the toilet, after a runny nose, and after animals or playing outside. Washing at every moment is not needed. That is called targeted hygiene.

items.p: In the haldi test, where did the yellow stay longest after a quick wash?
opts: On the middle of the palms
Between the fingers, round the thumbs and under the nails
On the backs of the wrists only
items.why: The middle of the palm gets rubbed most. The gaps between fingers, the thumbs and under nails are easy to miss. Picking 'palms' usually means thinking the part you look at is the part that is dirtiest.
items.context: In the haldi test, you rub oil and haldi on your hands as pretend germs, then wash them in different ways.

items.p: Match each body part to a way of caring for it.
items.why: Brushing removes mouth bacteria that make acid. Short nails leave nowhere for germs to hide. Earwax cleans itself out, and poking can hurt the eardrum. Chappals stop worm larvae in dirty soil getting in through feet.

items.p: You need to sneeze, and there is no tissue. What is best?
opts: Sneeze into your hand and carry on
Hold the sneeze in for as long as you can
items.why: Your elbow catches most of the drops, and you don't touch things with your elbow. Picking 'into your hand' is very common. But then your hand spreads the germs to everything you touch, unless you wash straight away.

items.p: A soap molecule has a head that loves water and a tail that loves ____.
items.why: The tail sticks into oil and grease. The head sticks to water. That is how soap can hold both.

items.p: Most microbes are harmful germs.
items.why: False. Only a small number of microbes cause illness. Most are harmless, and many help us, like the microbes in curd and the soil.

items.p: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water. Which of these is the best way to stop them at home?
opts: Empty pots, trays, coolers and tyres of still water once a week
Leave a bucket of water out for them
items.why: Mosquito eggs take about a week to become flying mosquitoes. Emptying still water every week stops them growing up. Picking 'perfume' usually means thinking smells are the problem, as people did long ago. Mosquitoes come from water, not smells.

items.p: Why should you dry your hands after washing?
opts: Wet hands pass on germs more easily than dry hands
items.why: Wet hands pick up and pass on germs more easily. A clean towel or air drying helps. Picking 'water makes germs grow bigger' mixes up washing with leaving food damp for days, as in the bread test.

items.p: Write two moments in your day when washing your hands matters most. Say why for each one.
items.a: Any two good moments with reasons. For example: before I eat, so germs on my hands do not go into my mouth. After the toilet, so germs from waste do not spread.
items.why: Any two key moments with a reason about germs travelling are right.

items.p: Your private parts are covered by your underwear. Write two things that are true about them.
items.a: They are kept clean, by washing every day. They are private, and my body belongs to me. If a touch ever feels wrong, I say no, get away and tell a grown-up I trust.
items.why: Clean, private, and your own. A child is never in trouble for telling a trusted grown-up.

items.p: Draw a soap molecule. Label its water-loving head and its oil-loving tail.
items.a: A shape like a tadpole: a round head labelled 'loves water' and a long tail labelled 'loves oil'.
items.why: Two different ends is the whole secret of soap.
items.art: An empty box with the words 'head' and 'tail' as hints at either end.

items.p: Who helps keep a whole town free of germs?
opts: Sanitation workers, health workers, families and doctors, all together
items.why: Clean drains, safe water, rubbish taken away and clean habits at home all matter. Picking 'only doctors' is common. But doctors mostly treat illness. Sanitation workers and health workers help stop it starting.

items.p: Look at the chart from the haldi test. The child scored how much yellow was left, from 0 (none) to 5 (all). Which way of washing worked best?
items.why: Soap for 20 seconds left the least yellow. Picking 'soap, 5 seconds' usually means thinking soap works instantly. Soap needs time and rubbing to break up all the oil.
items.context: In the haldi test, you rub oil and haldi on your hands as pretend germs. Then you wash in three different ways, coating your hands again each time.

chart.title: Made-up example: yellow left after washing, from 0 (none) to 5 (all)

items.p: In the haldi test, why must you coat your hands with the same amount of oil and haldi each time?
opts: To make it a fair test
items.why: If you used more haldi one time, you would not know whether the washing or the amount caused the difference. Picking 'it does not matter' means missing the idea of a fair test: change only one thing.

items.p: In the pepper test, black pepper floats on water. A soapy finger touches the middle, and the pepper rushes to the edges. Why?
opts: The pepper is scared of soap
Soap weakens the pull between water molecules in the middle, so the stronger pull at the edges drags the pepper outwards
The soap pushes the pepper with a wave
items.why: The top of the water acts like a stretched skin. Soap breaks that skin in the middle. The rest of the skin pulls back to the edges and carries the pepper with it. Germs on your hands are different. Soap has to touch them, and scrubbing lifts them off. Then the water washes them away.
items.context: In the pepper test, you sprinkle black pepper on a plate of water. Then you touch the middle with a clean finger, and then with a soapy finger.

items.p: The pepper test shows that soap scares germs away from your hands.
items.why: False. The pepper moves because soap changes the water's surface. Real soap cleans by wrapping oil and germs and letting water carry them away. That needs rubbing and rinsing.

items.p: In the jar test, a jar of oil and water is shaken. Within a minute, the oil floats back to the top. A second jar has soap added, and it stays cloudy for many minutes. Why?
opts: Soap molecules wrap tiny drops of oil, so they stay mixed in the water
The second jar was shaken harder
items.why: Soap tails hold the oil and heads hold the water, so tiny oil drops stay spread through the water. Picking 'shaken harder' is a good thought about fairness. That is why both jars must be shaken for the same time.
items.context: In the jar test, you shake oil and water in two jars, and add soap to only one.

items.p: A tiny ball of soap molecules, with oil trapped inside, is called a ____.
items.why: Micelles are how soap carries oil and germs away in the rinse water.

items.p: How does soap destroy a flu virus?
opts: Its tails push into the virus's oily coat and break it apart
items.why: Flu viruses wear an oily coat made of molecules like soap's. Soap tails slip in and pull it apart. Picking 'poisons' is natural, because we think of cleaners as poisons. Soap works more like a crowbar than a poison.

items.p: Sort these into the right group.
cats: Germs that can make us ill
items: the microbes in curd
Helpful or harmless microbes
the cholera germ in dirty water
Germs that can make us ill
microbes that turn leaves into soil
Helpful or harmless microbes
the virus that causes flu
Germs that can make us ill
most microbes living on your skin
Helpful or harmless microbes
the malaria germ carried by mosquitoes
Germs that can make us ill
items.why: Most microbes are helpful or harmless. Only some are germs.

items.p: Washing with soap removes mostly which microbes?
opts: The visitors picked up from things you touched
Every single microbe on your skin
items.why: Visitors sit on top of the skin and wash off. Most residents live deeper in the skin's folds and stay. Picking 'every single microbe' is common. That would actually be bad for skin.

items.p: Semmelweis's clue came from comparing two wards. Why was the midwives' ward so important?
opts: It showed that the same building could be much safer, so something in the doctors' ward was different
items.why: Without a safer ward to compare with, nobody would have known the fever could be stopped. The midwives' careful work was the clue. Picking 'better beds' is a fair guess, but the beds, food and sheets were the same.
items.context: In Vienna in 1847, one maternity ward was run by doctors and students, and the other by midwives. Far more mothers caught a fever in the doctors' ward.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: saw 'little animals' through his home-made lenses in the 1670s
made doctors wash in chlorine water in 1847
showed cholera spread through one water pump in 1854
first saw the cholera germ, in 1854
items.why: Each person added one piece. Germ theory was built by many people over about 350 years.

items.p: Is warm water needed to wash germs off your hands?
opts: No, cold and warm water work about the same. The soap and rubbing do the work.
items.why: In a 2017 study, cold and warm water removed germs about equally well. Picking 'boiling' mixes up washing hands with boiling drinking water. Boiling water kills germs, but it would burn your skin.

items.p: Explain to a younger cousin why soap cleans better than water. Use the words oil, head and tail.
items.a: Germs stick in the oil on our skin. Water slides off oil. A soap molecule has a head that loves water and a tail that loves oil. The tails grab the oil and the heads grab the water, so the water can wash the oil and germs away.
items.why: A good answer says the germs are in oil, water cannot hold oil, and soap holds both.

items.p: Reetha makes foam in water. What does that tell you about what is inside it?
items.a: Reetha has soap-like molecules, called saponins, with a water-loving end and an oil-loving end. That is why it foams and cleans.
items.why: Foam is a sign of soap-like molecules holding air and water.

items.p: Draw a micelle: a ring of soap molecules around a blob of oil. Show which way the heads and tails point.
items.a: A ring of tadpoles with their tails pointing into an oil blob in the middle, and their heads pointing out into the water.
items.why: Tails in the oil, heads in the water.
items.art: An empty circle labelled 'oil blob' in the middle of a blue box labelled 'water'.

items.p: Why does emptying flowerpot trays once a week stop mosquitoes, even though mosquitoes can still lay eggs?
opts: The eggs need about a week in water to become flying mosquitoes, so emptying the water first stops them
items.why: Eggs become wrigglers, then flying mosquitoes, in about a week in warm weather. Tip the water out before that, and none grow up. Picking 'mosquitoes hate empty pots' misses the real reason: their young need water to grow.

items.p: Look at the chart of Semmelweis's numbers. What happened after hand-washing began in May 1847?
opts: Deaths fell from about 18 out of 100 to about 2 out of 100
items.why: The numbers fell sharply after washing began, and stayed low. Picking 'nobody counted' misses how important counting was. The careful counts were the evidence.
items.context: In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis made doctors in one Vienna maternity ward wash their hands in chlorine water before touching mothers. He wrote down how many mothers died of childbed fever each month.

chart.title: Mothers who died of childbed fever in the doctors' ward, out of every 100

show.art: A doctor in an 1840s coat walking from a dissecting room straight to a mother's bed, without washing.
show.caption: Before May 1847: no washing.

show.art: The same doctor washing his hands in a basin of chlorine water by the ward door.
show.caption: From May 1847: washing in chlorine water.

items.p: In April 1847, about 18 out of 100 mothers in the doctors' ward died. By June, about 2 out of 100 did. That is ____ times fewer.
items.why: 18 divided by 2 is 9. So about 9 times fewer mothers died after washing began.

items.p: Semmelweis chose chlorine water because ordinary soap did not remove the smell of the cutting room from his hands. What was he using the smell as?
opts: A sign that something invisible was still on his hands
A way to make his hands smell nice
A test of the soap's colour
items.why: He could not see the 'particles' he suspected. The smell was a clue that something stayed. Picking 'smell nice' misses that he was using his nose as a measuring tool. Scientists often use clues to study things they cannot see.

items.p: Many doctors in 1847 refused to wash. Which reason was the LEAST scientific?
opts: Nobody had yet seen the germs
Semmelweis could not explain why washing worked
A gentleman's hands could not possibly be dirty
Chlorine water made their hands sore
items.why: Saying a gentleman's hands cannot be dirty is pride, not evidence. The other reasons were real problems, even if the numbers already showed washing worked. Science should follow the evidence, even when it is uncomfortable.

items.p: The cell walls in your body are built from molecules with water-loving heads and oil-loving tails, like soap.
items.why: True. Cell membranes are two layers of such molecules, heads out and tails in. The oily coat of flu viruses is built the same way, which is why soap breaks it.

items.p: If soap can break a virus's oily coat, why doesn't it break the cells of your hands?
opts: The top layer of your skin is made of tough, dead cells packed tightly, so soap cannot reach the living cells
Your cells are made of metal
items.why: Your skin's top layer is a tough wall of dead cells. Soap can dry it by removing some oil, but it cannot get through to living cells. Picking 'it breaks them all' is a sensible worry, but skin is built to stop that.

items.p: Robert Koch is often given credit for finding the cholera germ in 1884. Why do many scientists say Filippo Pacini deserves credit too?
opts: Pacini saw and described the cholera germ in 1854, thirty years earlier, but few people noticed
items.why: Pacini described it first, in Italy, but most scientists then believed in bad air and ignored him. Today the germ's scientific name includes his name and the year 1854. Picking 'there is no reason' misses that credit often goes to whoever convinces the world, not who saw it first.

items.p: Some people say homes today are 'too clean', causing allergies. Which is the most careful thing to say?
opts: Stop washing hands, so children meet more germs
Scientists still argue. Many think meeting harmless outdoor microbes helps, while washing at key moments still saves lives
Allergies have nothing to do with microbes, for sure
items.why: The idea is still debated. No study shows that washing hands before meals causes allergies. Picking 'stop washing' takes a debated idea and turns it into dangerous advice. The careful answer says what is known and what is not.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether reetha water or soap cleans oil off a steel plate better. What will you change? What will you keep the same?
items.a: Change only the cleaner: reetha water on one plate, soap on another. Keep the same amount of oil, the same plates, the same amount of water, and the same number of wipes. Then compare how greasy each plate feels, or how a tissue looks after wiping.
items.why: A good fair test changes one thing and names at least three things kept the same.

items.p: Anna in the story was only nine, but she helped. Write about a time when someone younger or less important noticed something that grown-ups missed.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: my little sister noticed the tap was dripping when nobody else did, and we saved a bucket of water every day.
items.why: This links the story to how anyone can notice evidence, and how good science listens to everyone.
items.context: In this unit's story, The Basin by the Door, Anna is a nine-year-old girl who helps her mother wash hospital sheets in Vienna in 1847.

items.p: In 1896, Ernest Hankin found that Ganga water killed cholera germs in his tests. What do many scientists think was doing it?
opts: Viruses that attack only bacteria, called bacteriophages
items.why: Bacteriophages were found about 20 years later, and they kill bacteria. Nobody can be sure, because his water samples are gone. Picking 'fish' is a fun guess, but his filtered water had no fish in it. River water today still needs boiling before drinking.

items.p: Microbes were on Earth for billions of years before any animal. Do you think they matter only for what they do for people? Give a reason.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer with a reason. For example: no, they matter for themselves, because they are living things with their own lives, and the whole Earth depends on them, not just people.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason.

items.p: Put these discoveries in the order they happened, earliest first.
items: Fracastoro writes about invisible seeds of disease (1546)
Leeuwenhoek sees 'little animals' (1670s)
Semmelweis's hand-washing basin (1847)
Koch grows the cholera germ (1884)
items.why: Germ theory grew slowly over more than 300 years, each person building on others.

items.p: Which of these is NOT a way animals keep clean?
opts: Bees carrying dead bees out of the hive
Mosquitoes laying eggs in still water
items.why: Laying eggs in water is how mosquitoes have young, not a way of keeping clean. The other three really are ways animals keep themselves or their homes clean.

items.p: Some people say dirt is just 'something in the wrong place'. Do you agree? Give one example for and one against.
items.a: A balanced answer. For example: for, soil is good in a garden but dirty on a plate. Against, some things, like germs in drinking water, are harmful almost anywhere we meet them.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What counts is a reason for each side.

items.p: Why might plants like reetha make soap-like molecules?
opts: To protect themselves from insects and fungi
So people can wash their hair
items.why: Saponins taste bitter and can harm insects and fungi, which helps protect the plant. Picking 'so people can wash' is a very human-centred idea. Plants were making saponins long before people existed.

experiments.title: The Haldi Germ Test: water or soap?
experiments.question: Does soap clean pretend germs off hands better than water? Does rubbing for longer help?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Rank the three ways from best to worst: water only for 20 seconds, soap for 5 seconds, soap for 20 seconds.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the way of washing. Use the same amount of oil and haldi each time, measured with the same spoon. Use the same tap, and count the seconds out loud. Wash off completely between rounds, then coat again.

materials.item: half a teaspoon of cooking oil for each round (coconut or any oil)
a pinch of haldi (turmeric powder) for each round
soap: a bar or liquid handwash
a tap, or a mug and bucket of water
an old towel you don't mind turning yellow
a clock or phone that shows seconds

experiments.safety: Haldi stains clothes yellow, so wear old clothes and roll up sleeves. Keep oily hands away from eyes. The floor near the tap can get slippery, so wipe it dry.

schedule.what: Coat hands three times and wash three ways. Score the yellow each time and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw your hands after each wash and colour where yellow stayed. Then draw a bar for each way of washing.

flow.do: 1. Put the oil, haldi, soap and towel near the tap. 2. Ask your child to rank the three ways of washing, best first.
flow.say: Real germs are far too small to see. So today, haldi in oil is our pretend germ. Germs on real hands sit in the skin's own oil, just like this. Which way of washing do you think will work best?
flow.kid: Haldi in oil is your pretend germ. Real germs hide in your skin's oil. Guess which wash will work best.
flow.context: This is the first step of the haldi germ test. You use oil and haldi as pretend germs and test three ways of washing.

flow.do: 1. Put half a teaspoon of oil in your child's palms. 2. Add a pinch of haldi. 3. Rub all over both hands, backs, between fingers and under nails, for 10 seconds. 4. Rinse under water only for 20 seconds, counting out loud, rubbing as normal. 5. Pat dry with the old towel.
flow.say: Round one: water only, for 20 seconds. Count with me. Now look. How much yellow is left, from 0 for none to 5 for all of it?
flow.kid: Rub oil and haldi on both hands. Rinse with water only. Count to 20. How much yellow is left? Score it, 0 to 5.

ask.q: What do the water drops do on your oily hands?

flow.do: 1. Wash off fully with soap and dry. 2. Coat again with the same oil and haldi, the same way. 3. This time use soap, but rub for only 5 seconds, then rinse. 4. Score the yellow.
flow.say: Round two: soap, but only 5 seconds. Same oil, same haldi. Only one thing changes. Score it.
flow.kid: Coat your hands again, the same way. Now soap for just 5 seconds. Rinse. Score the yellow, 0 to 5.
flow.parent: Haldi dyes skin a little, so a faint yellow tint may stay even after a good wash. Score the clumps and patches of powder, not the faint colour. A pale tint that will not wash off is the dye, not the pretend germs. The soap bar will turn a little yellow too. Rinse it at the end.

flow.do: 1. Wash fully, dry, and coat again. 2. Now wash with soap for 20 seconds: palms, backs, between fingers, round each thumb, fingertips, under nails and wrists. Sing Happy Birthday twice. 3. Rinse well and score.
flow.say: Round three: soap for 20 seconds, every part. Sing Happy Birthday twice while you rub. Now score it. Where did the yellow stay longest?
flow.kid: Coat again. Soap for 20 seconds. Rub every part, even thumbs and nails. Sing Happy Birthday twice. Score it.

check.q: Which wash usually leaves the least yellow?
options: Water only, 20 seconds
Soap, 5 seconds
Soap, 20 seconds
check.why: Soap holds oil and water both, and 20 seconds of rubbing gives it time to break up all the oil, even in the gaps. Picking water only usually means thinking rubbing is all that matters. Picking soap for 5 seconds usually means thinking soap works instantly.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart with one bar for each way of washing, as tall as its score.
flow.say: Let's turn the scores into a picture. A shorter bar means less yellow left, so a cleaner hand.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each wash. Make it as tall as the score. Short bar means clean hands!

chart.title: Made-up example results: yellow left after washing, from 0 (none) to 5 (all)
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: soap for 20 seconds cleans best. What I saw: water left a score of 4, and soap for 20 seconds left 0. Why: the haldi was stuck in oil, water slides off oil, and soap holds both oil and water.

experiments.context: This is the haldi germ test. You coat your hands in oil and haldi as pretend germs, then wash three ways to see which cleans best.
