experiments.title: Pepper on the Run
experiments.question: What does soap do to the surface of water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When you touch soapy water's middle with a soapy finger, what will the pepper do?
experiments.fair_test: Touch the water twice: once with a clean, dry finger and once with a soapy finger. Use the same plate, the same water and the same amount of pepper. Use fresh water for every new try, because soap stays in the water.

materials.item: a wide plate or steel thali with a rim
water, about 2 cm deep
ground black pepper, about half a teaspoon
a drop of liquid handwash or dishwashing liquid, or a wet bar of soap

experiments.safety: Keep pepper away from eyes and noses. Wash hands after.

schedule.what: Sprinkle pepper on water and touch it with a clean finger, then a soapy one.

experiments.record: Draw the plate before and after the soapy finger. Write one sentence about what the pepper did.

flow.do: 1. Pour water into the plate, about 2 cm deep. 2. Wait until it is still. 3. Shake black pepper all over the top, until the surface is speckled. 4. Your child touches the middle with a clean, dry finger.
flow.say: Touch the middle with a clean finger. Watch the pepper. Did much happen?
flow.kid: Pour water on a plate. Shake pepper on top. Touch the middle with a clean finger. What happens?
flow.context: This is the first step of Pepper on the Run. You float pepper on water and see what soap does to the water's surface.

flow.do: 1. Put a drop of liquid soap on your child's fingertip, or rub it on a wet bar of soap. 2. Touch the middle of the water again and hold still.
flow.say: Now put soap on your fingertip and touch the middle again. Watch closely!
flow.kid: Put soap on your fingertip. Touch the middle again. Watch closely!

good: It ran away from my finger.
It moved out in a circle.

flow.parent: The pepper shoots to the edges in under a second. If nothing happens, the water already had soap in it, or the plate had soap on it. Rinse the plate well, use fresh water, and try again. The trick works only once per plate of water.

flow.do: Explain what really happened.
flow.say: The top of water acts like a stretched skin, because water molecules pull on each other. Soap squeezes in between them in the middle and weakens the pull there. The rest of the surface pulls outwards, like a balloon popping, and carries the pepper with it. The pepper isn't scared. It is pulled.
flow.kid: Water's top is like a stretched skin. Soap weakens it in the middle. The rest pulls out, carrying the pepper.

check.q: Why did the pepper rush to the edges?
options: Soap weakened the water's surface in the middle, so the rest pulled the pepper outwards
The pepper was scared of the soap
The finger made a big wave
check.why: Water molecules at the surface pull on each other. Soap weakens that pull in the middle, so the stronger pull further out drags the pepper away. Picking 'scared of soap' is a story people often tell, and it can make children think germs run from soap. They don't. Soap has to wrap germs and the water rinses them away. The clean finger made the same kind of wave, and the pepper hardly moved.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Like a scientist: what do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: soap changes the surface of water. What I saw: with a clean finger the pepper stayed, with a soapy finger it shot to the edges. Why: soap weakens the pull between water molecules in the middle.

experiments.context: In this short experiment you float black pepper on water, then touch it with a soapy finger. It shows that soap molecules change the water's surface.

experiments.title: Oil, Water and Soap in a Jar
experiments.question: Can soap make oil and water mix?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After shaking, which jar will stay mixed longer: oil and water, or oil, water and soap?
experiments.fair_test: Use two jars the same size. Put the same amount of water and oil in each. Add soap to only one jar. Shake both for the same time, 10 seconds, then put them down together and start the timer.
results_table: Seconds until a clear oil layer is back on top

materials.item: two clear jars or plastic bottles with tight lids, the same size
water, half a cup for each jar
cooking oil, 2 tablespoons for each jar
a pinch of haldi, to colour the oil yellow so it is easy to see (optional)
half a teaspoon of dishwashing liquid or liquid handwash
a clock or phone that shows seconds

experiments.safety: Close lids tightly. Use plastic bottles if a small child will shake them.

schedule.what: Shake oil and water in two jars, one with soap, and time how long each stays mixed.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both jars straight after shaking, and after 2 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Stir a pinch of haldi into the oil, so the oil turns yellow. 2. Put half a cup of water and 2 tablespoons of yellow oil in each jar. 3. Add half a teaspoon of soap to jar 2 only. 4. Close both lids tightly.
flow.say: Look: the yellow oil floats on top of the water in a layer. Oil and water don't mix. Jar 2 also has soap.
flow.kid: Put water and yellow oil in two jars. Add soap to jar 2 only. See the oil float on top?
flow.context: This is the first step of the jar test. You find out whether soap can make oil and water mix.

flow.do: 1. Shake both jars hard for 10 seconds, at the same time if you can. 2. Put them down side by side and start the timer. 3. Watch for a clear yellow layer coming back on top. Write down the seconds for each jar.
flow.say: Shake them both for 10 seconds. Now watch. Which jar separates first?
flow.kid: Shake both jars for 10 seconds. Put them down. Start the timer. Which one separates first?
flow.parent: Jar 1 usually shows a clear oil layer again within 1 to 3 minutes. Jar 2 stays cloudy and creamy for 10 minutes or more. If jar 2 is still cloudy at 10 minutes, stop the timer and write 'more than 600 seconds'. A creamy band may rise to the top of jar 2, but it stays cloudy, not clear. Some foam on top is normal. If jar 2 separates fast too, add a little more soap and shake again. Bar soap scraped into flakes works too, but slowly, so liquid soap is best.

flow.do: Explain what is in the cloudy jar.
flow.say: The cloudy jar is full of millions of tiny oil drops, each one wrapped in soap molecules. Tails in the oil, heads in the water. That is exactly how soap carries oil off your hands.
flow.kid: The cloudy jar is full of tiny oil drops. Each is wrapped in soap. That is how soap cleans hands!

check.q: Why did the soapy jar stay cloudy?
options: Soap molecules wrapped tiny drops of oil, so they stayed mixed in the water
The soap made the oil heavier
Jar 2 was shaken harder
check.why: Each tiny oil drop is wrapped in soap molecules, tails in and heads out, so it can stay in the water. Picking 'shaken harder' is a good fairness worry. That is why both jars were shaken for the same 10 seconds.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Like a scientist: what do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: soap helps oil mix with water. What I saw: the jar without soap separated in about 40 seconds, the soapy one stayed cloudy for over 10 minutes. Why: soap holds oil with one end and water with the other.

experiments.context: In this experiment you shake oil and water in two jars, adding soap to only one. It shows how soap holds oil and water together.

experiments.title: The Bread Test: what do hands leave behind?
experiments.question: Do unwashed hands carry living things we can't see? Does washing help?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which slice will grow spots of mould first and most: not touched, dirty hands, water-only hands or soap-washed hands?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except how the hands were cleaned. Use slices from the same loaf, the same bags, the same drops of water and the same cupboard. Rub each slice for the same 10 seconds.

materials.item: 4 slices of bread or pav from the same packet, best from a local bakery
4 zip bags or 4 small boxes with tight lids
a marker pen for labels
a clean spoon or tongs
soap and water

experiments.safety: Never open the bags once sealed. Mould can make people with asthma or allergies ill. At the end, throw the bags away still sealed and wash your hands.

schedule.what: Touch the slices in four ways, seal them in bags, and put them in a warm, dark cupboard.
Look through the bags without opening them. Count and draw any spots.
Look again. Count and draw the spots on each slice.
Look one last time. Fill in the table, draw a bar chart, and throw the sealed bags away.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 3, 5 and 7. Draw each slice. On day 7, draw a bar chart of the spots on each slice.

flow.do: 1. Label the four bags: Not touched, Dirty hands, Water only, Soap. 2. Use the spoon to put slice 1 into 'Not touched' without touching it. Seal it.
flow.say: Mould is a tiny fungus, a living thing. Its seeds, called spores, are too small to see. If they land on damp bread, they grow into spots we can see. Let's see what our hands carry.
flow.kid: Label four bags. Use a spoon to put one slice in 'Not touched'. Do not touch it! Seal it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bread test. You touch slices of bread with hands cleaned in different ways, and watch what grows over a week.

flow.do: 1. Before washing, after play or after handling coins, your child rubs both hands on slice 2 for 10 seconds. Bag it. 2. Rinse hands under water only for 5 seconds, then rub slice 3. Bag it. 3. Wash with soap for 20 seconds, dry on a clean towel, and rub slice 4. Bag it. 4. Add 3 drops of water to each bag and seal tightly.
flow.say: Rub the dirty hands slice for 10 seconds. Now water only. Now soap for 20 seconds. Same 10-second rub each time.
flow.kid: Rub one slice with dirty hands. Rinse with water. Rub the next. Wash with soap. Rub the last. Seal them.
flow.parent: Bread with preservatives, which is most packet bread, can take 10 days or more to grow mould. Fresh bakery bread or pav works fastest, often in 4 to 6 days. Keep the bags in a warm, dark cupboard, not the fridge.

flow.do: Put all four bags together in a warm, dark cupboard.
flow.say: Now we wait. Living things need time to grow.
flow.kid: Put all four bags in a warm, dark cupboard. Now wait. Living things need time.
flow.wait: Look again on day 3, day 5 and day 7, without opening the bags.

flow.do: On days 3, 5 and 7, look through the bags without opening them. Count the spots of mould on each slice and write them in the table.
flow.say: Count the spots on each slice. Green, black, white or orange spots are all mould.
flow.kid: Look through the bags. Do not open them! Count the spots on each slice. Write them down.
flow.parent: Results are often messy. The 'dirty hands' slice usually grows most. The 'not touched' slice can still grow some, because spores float in the air everywhere. Water-only is usually in between. If nothing has grown by day 7, wait until day 10. If the soap slice grows a lot, ask: were the hands dried on a clean towel? That is a real result to talk about, not a failure.

check.q: Why can the 'not touched' slice still grow a little mould?
options: Mould spores float in the air everywhere, so some land on it anyway
The spoon was magic
Bread makes mould by itself, from nothing
check.why: Mould spores are in the air all around us. Some land on every slice. Picking 'bread makes mould from nothing' is what many people believed until Louis Pasteur showed, in the 1860s, that living things come only from other living things.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, draw a bar chart of the spots on each slice. 2. Ask for three sentences: what I think, what I saw, why. 3. Throw the bags away still sealed, and wash hands.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each slice. Then say what you think, what you saw and why. Throw the bags away sealed.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: dirty hands carry living things we cannot see. What I saw: the dirty hands slice had 9 spots, the soap slice had 2. Why: soap washed most spores and microbes off my hands.

experiments.context: In this week-long experiment, you touch bread with hands cleaned in different ways. Then you watch what grows. It shows that hands carry living things too small to see.

activities.title: How Often Do You Touch Your Face?

materials.item: paper and a pencil for tally marks
a clock or phone timer

schedule.what: Count face touches for 10 minutes, then work out how many in an hour.

activities.record: Make tally marks for each touch. Write which part was touched most: eyes, nose, mouth or other.

flow.do: Explain the task. Your child will count your face touches, and you will count theirs, without saying when.
flow.say: Germs get in most easily through the eyes, nose and mouth. Hands carry them there. So how often do our hands touch our faces? Let's spy on each other for 10 minutes.
flow.kid: Hands carry germs to your eyes, nose and mouth. How often do you touch your face? Let's count!
flow.context: This is the first step of the face-touch count. You and a grown-up secretly count how often each of you touches your face in 10 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer for 10 minutes. 2. Carry on reading, drawing or watching something. 3. Each person makes a tally mark every time they see the other touch their face. Mark E for eyes, N for nose, M for mouth, O for other.
flow.say: Just do what you normally do. I'll count yours, and you count mine.
flow.kid: Read or draw as normal. Make a mark each time your grown-up touches their face. E, N, M or O.
flow.parent: Most people are surprised. A study in 2015 watched 26 medical students on video, and found they touched their faces about 23 times an hour. Almost half the touches were on the eyes, nose or mouth. Playing alone, a child can count a family member or a person in a video.

flow.do: Count the tallies. Multiply by 6 to estimate touches in one hour.
flow.say: There are six lots of 10 minutes in an hour. So we multiply by 6. How many face touches in a whole day?
flow.kid: Count the marks. Multiply by 6 for one hour. Is it more than you guessed?

check.q: Why does it matter how often we touch our faces?
options: Hands carry germs to the eyes, nose and mouth, where they get in easily
Touching your face makes it dirty-looking
It doesn't matter at all
check.why: The eyes, nose and mouth have soft, wet linings that germs can get through. Hands bring germs there. That is why washing hands before eating or rubbing eyes matters. Picking 'dirty-looking' is about how things look, not germs. How the body fights germs that do get in is in the immune system unit.

flow.think: We touch our faces without noticing. What else do your hands do without you deciding?

activities.context: This is a counting activity. You count how often people touch their faces, because that is how hands carry germs into the body.

setup.caption: 2. Make a tally mark every time the other person touches their face.

activities.title: Reetha Foam: a plant that makes soap

materials.item: 4 or 5 dried reetha (soapnut) shells, from a kirana or ayurvedic shop, or 1 teaspoon of shikakai powder
a cup of warm water, not hot
two small steel plates
a few drops of cooking oil
a bar of soap and a tissue or old cloth

activities.safety: Reetha water stings badly in the eyes. Keep it away from faces. A grown-up helps squeeze the shells. If it gets in an eye, rinse with plenty of clean water.

schedule.what: Soak reetha, make foam, and test it against soap on an oily plate.

activities.record: Draw the foam. Write which cleaned the oily plate better: reetha water, soap or plain water.

flow.do: 1. Break the reetha shells into pieces and take out any hard black seeds. 2. Drop the shells into a cup of warm water. 3. Leave them to soak for at least 15 minutes. Start this an hour before, or in the morning, if you can.
flow.say: This dry fruit comes from the soapnut tree. People in India have washed hair and silk with it for hundreds of years. Let's find out why.
flow.kid: Break the reetha shells. Take out the black seeds. Put the shells in warm water. Wait.
flow.context: This is the first step of the reetha foam activity. You soak dried soapnuts to see if a plant can make soap.

flow.do: 1. Rub a few drops of oil on both steel plates. 2. Wipe one plate with plain water only, using your fingers. 3. Feel it. 4. Leave the other oily plate for the reetha.
flow.say: Feel this plate after plain water. Still greasy? Now let's see what reetha does.
flow.kid: Rub oil on two plates. Wash one with plain water. Is it still greasy? Keep the other one.

flow.do: 1. Squeeze the soaked shells in the water with your fingers, again and again. 2. Watch foam appear. 3. Use the reetha water to wash the second oily plate. 4. Wipe both plates with a tissue and compare. 5. If you like, compare with a third plate washed with soap.
flow.say: Look at that foam! Reetha has soap-like molecules called saponins. Each one has a water-loving end and an oil-loving end, just like soap. Does it clean the oil?
flow.kid: Squeeze the shells in the water. See the foam? Wash the oily plate with it. Is it cleaner?
flow.parent: Squeezing for 1 to 2 minutes usually makes a good foam. If the shells have soaked only a few minutes, rub them hard between your fingers. Foam still comes, just less. Reetha cleans oil off steel well, though usually a little less strongly than dishwashing liquid. If the foam is weak, soak the shells longer, or overnight. Keep the leftover water for washing a cloth. Throw the used shells in compost.

flow.do: Talk about why the plant makes saponins.
flow.say: The soapnut tree did not make saponins for us. They taste bitter and can harm insects and fungi. So they probably protect the fruit. People learned to borrow them.
flow.kid: The tree did not make reetha soap for us. It probably protects the fruit from insects and fungi.

check.q: Why does reetha water foam and clean?
options: It has soap-like molecules, with a water-loving end and an oil-loving end
It is full of tiny bubbles of air from the tree
It is just very hot water
check.why: Saponins hold oil and water, like soap, and they hold air in foam bubbles too. Picking 'air from the tree' mixes up foam with something stored inside the fruit. The foam forms only when you squeeze it in water. The water was only warm, so heat was not the reason.

flow.think: What other plants might make their own chemicals to protect themselves?

activities.context: This activity uses reetha, the soapnut, a dried fruit sold in Indian shops. You make foam from it and test whether a plant's own soap can clean oil.

setup.caption: 1. Break the reetha shells into warm water. Soak for 15 minutes.

setup.art: Fingers squeezing soaked reetha shells in a cup, white foam rising up.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze the shells again and again. Foam appears.

setup.art: Two steel plates side by side, one still shiny with oil and one clean after reetha water.
setup.caption: 3. Wash an oily plate with the reetha water. Compare it with plain water.

activities.title: Clean Street Survey and the Weekly Dry Day

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
chappals or shoes

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along. Do not touch rubbish, drains or animal droppings. Look, don't touch. Wash hands with soap when you get home.

schedule.what: Walk round home and street. List germ spots and clean spots. Fix one germ spot.

activities.record: A two-column list: germ spots and clean spots. Draw the one germ spot you fixed.

flow.do: Explain what you are looking for.
flow.say: Germs spread to whole families through dirty water, flies on food, and mosquitoes. Today we are germ-spot detectives. We'll look for still water, open rubbish and uncovered food. We'll also look for clean spots.
flow.kid: You are a germ-spot detective! Look for still water, open rubbish and uncovered food. Look for clean spots too.
flow.context: This is the first step of the clean street survey. You look round your home and street for places where germs or mosquitoes could spread.

flow.do: 1. Look round the home first: kitchen, bathroom, balcony, roof. 2. Then the street. 3. Look for water standing in flowerpot trays, buckets, coolers, coconut shells, tyres and blocked drains. 4. Look for open rubbish, flies and uncovered food. 5. Notice covered water tanks, covered bins and swept steps too.
flow.say: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, even in a bottle cap. The eggs become flying mosquitoes in about a week. So any water left for a week is a mosquito nursery.
flow.kid: Look for still water anywhere. Even a bottle cap counts! Write each germ spot and clean spot down.
flow.parent: You may see tiny wriggling larvae in old water. Do not keep them. Tip the water onto dry soil, never into a drain. Many Indian cities run a weekly 'dry day', when families empty and scrub every water container.

flow.do: 1. With a grown-up, fix one germ spot at home today, for example tip out and scrub a flowerpot tray. 2. Choose one day of the week as your family's dry day. 3. Talk about who cleans the street.
flow.say: Who keeps our street clean? Let's find out their names if we can, and say thank you next time we see them.
flow.kid: Fix one germ spot with a grown-up. Pick a dry day each week. Who cleans your street? Say thank you!

check.q: Why do we empty still water once a week, not once a month?
options: Mosquito eggs become flying mosquitoes in about a week
Water goes bad on Sundays
Once a month would be too much work
check.why: In warm weather, eggs become larvae and then flying mosquitoes in about 7 to 10 days. Emptying the water every week stops them before they can fly. Picking 'too much work' is honest, but a month gives mosquitoes plenty of time to grow up.

flow.think: One flowerpot tray can grow mosquitoes for a whole building. Whose job is it to keep a street healthy?

activities.context: This is a walk round your home and street, looking for germ spots and clean spots. You also fix one germ spot and choose a weekly dry day against mosquitoes.

activities.title: How Do Animals Keep Clean?

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a window, balcony, garden or park where you can watch animals

activities.safety: Watch animals from a distance. Never touch street dogs, monkeys or cows. Wash hands after being outside.

schedule.what: Watch birds, cats, dogs, cows or monkeys. Note every way they clean themselves.

activities.record: Draw three animals cleaning. Write what each one did, and why you think it did it.

flow.do: Explain what to look for.
flow.say: People are not the only ones who keep clean. Today we watch other animals and see how they do it, in their own way and for their own reasons.
flow.kid: Watch animals near your home. How do they keep clean? Write or draw what you see.
flow.context: This is the first step of the animal cleaning watch. You watch birds, cats and other animals to see how they keep themselves clean.

flow.do: 1. Watch for 15 minutes, from a window, a balcony or a park. 2. Look for crows or sparrows bathing in water or dust, birds combing feathers with their beaks, cats licking fur, dogs shaking water off, cows flicking flies with their tails, or monkeys grooming each other.
flow.say: What is that bird doing with its beak? Why might a cat spend so long licking its fur?
flow.kid: Watch closely. Is a bird combing its feathers? Is a cat licking its fur? Draw it.
flow.parent: If you can't see animals today, watch a pet, or look at the cards in this unit about animals cleaning. Good answers: birds preen to keep feathers waterproof and tidy, and bathe in dust to get rid of tiny pests. Cats lick to clean and to cool down. Monkeys groom to remove insects and to be friends.

flow.do: Share what you saw.
flow.say: Bees in a hive have cleaner bees too. They clean the wax cells and carry dead bees out, so illness doesn't spread. Why do you think so many animals clean?
flow.kid: Bees have cleaner bees in the hive! Why do you think so many animals keep clean?

check.q: Why do birds take dust baths?
options: To help get rid of tiny pests in their feathers
Because they like being dirty
To change colour
check.why: Dust soaks up extra oil and helps shake off tiny pests like mites. Picking 'they like being dirty' is a very human way to see it. For a bird, dust is a cleaner, not dirt. That is a good example of dirt being something in the wrong place.

flow.think: A dust bath cleans a bird. Is dust dirty?

activities.context: This activity is a watch. You look at how birds, cats, cows and other animals keep themselves clean, in their own ways.

activities.title: My Body Care Map

materials.item: a big sheet of chart paper, or newspapers taped together
crayons or markers

schedule.what: Draw round your child. Label each outer body part with one care rule.

activities.record: A life-size poster of the outside of your body, with one care rule for each part.

flow.do: Your child lies on the paper while you draw round them with a marker.
flow.say: Let's make a map of you! Then we'll write how to look after each part.
flow.kid: Lie down on the paper. A grown-up draws round you. This is a map of you!
flow.context: This is the first step of the body care map. You draw round your body and label how to care for each outer part.

flow.do: 1. Label hair, eyes, ears, nose, mouth and teeth, hands and nails, skin, feet and private parts. 2. Next to each, write or draw one care rule. 3. Use the list in the parent note.
flow.say: What does each part need? For the ears, never poke inside, because earwax cleans itself out. What about teeth?
flow.kid: Label each part. Next to it, write one way to care for it. Teeth? Nails? Feet?
flow.parent: Care rules: hair, wash and comb, check for lice. Eyes, don't rub with dirty hands. Ears, never poke inside. Nose, blow into a hanky, then wash hands. Teeth, brush twice a day. Nails, keep short and clean. Skin, bathe often. Feet, wear chappals outside. Private parts: clean every day, private, and my body belongs to me. Say plainly: if any touch ever feels wrong, say no, get away and tell a trusted grown-up. It is never the child's fault.

flow.do: 1. Name three trusted grown-ups together and write them on the map. 2. Stick the map on the wall at your child's height.
flow.say: Who are three grown-ups you trust, who you could always tell anything? Let's write them on your map.
flow.kid: Name three grown-ups you trust. Write them on your map. Stick it on the wall.

check.q: Which is the safe way to care for your ears?
options: Wipe the outer ear with a cloth, and never poke anything inside
Clean deep inside with a matchstick every day
Pour oil in every morning
check.why: Earwax traps dust and germs and slowly moves out by itself. Poking can push wax deeper or hurt the eardrum. Picking a matchstick is very common, because many people think earwax is dirt. It is actually a cleaner.

activities.context: This activity makes a life-size map of your body. You label each outer part, such as hair, teeth, nails and feet, with one way to care for it.

activities.title: The Germ Detectives Washing Line

materials.item: a long piece of string, about 3 metres
8 cloth pegs or paper clips
8 cards or pieces of paper, and crayons

schedule.what: Make a timeline of how people discovered germs, on a washing line.

activities.record: A washing-line timeline with 8 cards. Circle the women and the people who were ignored at first.

flow.do: Tie the string across a room, like a washing line. Mark one end '1500' and the other 'today'.
flow.say: Nobody discovered germs in one day. It took about 350 years and many people. Let's hang their story on a washing line.
flow.kid: Tie the string across the room. One end is the year 1500. The other end is today.
flow.context: This is the first step of the germ detectives washing line. You make a timeline of how people found out that germs cause illness.

flow.do: 1. Make one card for each. A quick drawing or just the words is fine: 1546 Fracastoro's invisible seeds. 1670s Leeuwenhoek's little animals. 1847 Semmelweis and the midwives' ward. 1854 Pacini sees the cholera germ. 1854 John Snow's water pump. 1855 Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole nurse soldiers. 1860s Pasteur's flasks. 1884 Koch in Kolkata. 2. Peg each card where its year belongs.
flow.say: Let's put each card in the right place. Notice how long the gaps are.
flow.kid: Draw a picture for each card. Peg it on the line in the right place. Look at the gaps!
flow.parent: Space the cards by year. 1546 to the 1670s is a long gap. Most of the story crowds into 1840 to 1890. Point out that the midwives, Pacini and Mary Seacole were overlooked at first.

flow.do: Talk about who got the credit.
flow.say: Who is famous today? Who was ignored? Pacini saw the cholera germ 30 years before Koch, but hardly anyone listened. Why might that happen?
flow.kid: Who is famous? Who was ignored? Circle the people who were ignored at first.

check.q: Why did it take so long for people to accept germ theory?
options: Germs are too small to see without good microscopes, and many people trusted old ideas about bad air
Nobody was interested in illness
Germs did not exist before 1800
check.why: Without good microscopes, germs could not be seen, and the old idea of bad air seemed to fit. Changing a big idea takes evidence and time. Picking 'germs did not exist' mixes up when something was discovered with when it began. Microbes are billions of years old.

flow.think: Is there an idea everyone believes today that people might laugh at in 200 years?

activities.context: This activity makes a timeline on a string, like a washing line. It shows how people slowly found out that germs cause illness, from 1546 to 1884.

projects.title: Build a Tippy-Tap Hand-Washing Station

materials.item: a 2-litre plastic bottle with its cap
strong string, about 2 metres
a nail and a candle or stove, used only by a grown-up to make a small hole
a stick or broom handle, and two chairs, or a balcony railing to hang it from
a bar of soap with a hole made in it, or soap in an old net bag, on a string
a bucket or a patch of garden under it, to catch the water
a measuring jug or a 1-litre bottle

projects.safety: Only a grown-up heats the nail and makes the hole. Hold the hot nail with pliers or a thick cloth. Put the station where spilt water won't make a slippery floor.

schedule.what: A grown-up makes the hole. Tie and hang the bottle. Add the foot loop and the soap on a string. Test it.
Use it all day. Count how many washes one full bottle gives. Improve the design.

projects.record: Draw your tippy-tap and label each part. Write how many washes one bottle gave, and one thing you changed.

flow.do: Explain what a tippy-tap is.
flow.say: A tippy-tap is a hand-washing station made from a bottle and string. You tip it with your foot, so your dirty hands never touch a tap. Families and schools in many countries use them where there is no running water.
flow.kid: A tippy-tap is a tap made from a bottle. You tip it with your foot. Your hands touch nothing!
flow.context: This is the first step of the tippy-tap project. Over two days, you build a hand-washing station from a plastic bottle and string.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up heats the tip of a nail, holding it with pliers. 2. They push it through the bottle's shoulder, about 3 cm below the cap, to make one small hole. 3. Fill the bottle about three-quarters full, so the water stays below the hole. Screw the cap on loosely, so a little air can get in.
flow.say: The hole is near the top. Standing up, no water comes out. When we tip it, the water pours from the hole.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a small hole near the top. Fill the bottle three-quarters full. Cap on loosely.
flow.parent: Keep the hole small, about the size of a pencil lead, so the water comes out in a thin stream and lasts longer. If the stream stops after a moment, loosen the cap a little more.

flow.do: 1. Tie a string tightly round the middle of the bottle, and wrap tape over it so it cannot slip. 2. Hang the bottle by this string from a stick laid across two chairs, or from a railing, about at your child's waist, with the hole facing your child. 3. Tie a second string round the bottle's neck. Let it hang to the floor and tie a loop for a foot. 4. Hang the soap on its own string beside the bottle. 5. Put the bucket underneath.
flow.say: Press the loop with your foot. It pulls the neck down, so the bottle tips forward and water pours from the hole. Let go, and the heavy water at the bottom stands it up again.
flow.kid: Hang the bottle by its middle. Tie a foot loop to its neck. Hang the soap beside it. Press the loop!
flow.parent: The water sits low in the bottle, so it hangs upright by itself. If it tips over on its own, move the middle string a little higher. If it will not tip far enough to pour, make the foot string shorter.

flow.do: Test it. Your child washes their hands properly: wet, soap for 20 seconds, rinse. Check that hands touch only the soap.
flow.say: Wet your hands with your foot. Let go. Soap for 20 seconds. Rinse with your foot again. Did your hands touch anything else?
flow.kid: Press the loop to wet your hands. Soap for 20 seconds. Press again to rinse. Your hands touched only soap!

check.q: Why is the tippy-tap worked with a foot, not a hand?
options: So clean hands do not touch a dirty tap and pick germs up again
Because feet are stronger
It looks funny
check.why: A tap handle is touched by dirty hands before washing. Touching it again after washing puts germs back on clean hands. A foot loop avoids that. Picking 'feet are stronger' is true, but the bottle is light. The real reason is germs.

flow.do: 1. On day 2, everyone uses the tippy-tap all day. 2. Count every wash with a tally until the bottle is empty. 3. Talk about how to improve it: a hook for a towel, a cover against dust, a sign.
flow.say: How many washes did one bottle give? A running tap can pour a whole bottle in under a minute. What would you change?
flow.kid: Count every wash until the bottle is empty. How many? What would make it better?
flow.wait: Use it all of the next day, then count the washes.
flow.parent: Three-quarters of a 2-litre bottle is about 1,500 millilitres. It usually gives about 20 to 40 washes, depending on the hole size. That makes a good maths problem: divide the millilitres by the number of washes to find how much water one wash used.

projects.context: In this 2-day project, you build a tippy-tap. It is a hand-washing station made from a plastic bottle and string, tipped with your foot so clean hands touch nothing.

challenges.title: The Sneeze Catcher
challenges.problem: When someone sneezes, tiny drops fly out. Find out how far a pretend sneeze sprays, and which way of covering it stops the most drops.
constraints: Use only clean water in a spray bottle as the pretend sneeze. Never real sneezes.
Test each cover the same way: same spray bottle, same distance, same number of sprays.
Measure how far drops travel on newspaper, with a ruler or measuring tape.
materials: a plant spray bottle filled with clean water and a few drops of dark food colour or ink. Do not use haldi, which blocks the nozzle.
two big sheets of newspaper laid end to end on the floor
things to test as covers: a hand, an elbow in a sleeve, a hanky, a tissue, a cloth mask
general: Sneeze into a tissue, then throw it away and wash your hands.
If there is no tissue, sneeze into your elbow.
Wear a mask when you have a cold and must be near others.
creative: Design a 'sneeze pocket' sewn into a sleeve.
Make a family sign that reminds everyone: elbow, not hand.
Invent a way for a toddler, who can't remember, to learn the elbow sneeze, such as a song or a game.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own sneeze catcher. Draw it, test it with the spray bottle, and measure how far the drops go.

flow.do: 1. Lay the newspapers end to end on the floor. 2. Hold the spray bottle at the start of the paper, at your child's mouth height, pointing along the paper. 3. Spray once, firmly. 4. Measure the furthest coloured drop.
flow.say: This spray is our pretend sneeze. Let's see how far it goes with nothing in the way.
flow.kid: Spray the coloured water along the newspaper once. How far did the furthest drop go? Measure it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sneeze Catcher challenge. You use a spray bottle as a pretend sneeze to test which cover stops the most drops.

flow.do: 1. Test each cover in turn: hold it in front of the nozzle, like covering a sneeze, and spray once. 2. Measure the furthest drop each time. 3. Write the results down.
flow.say: Try the hand, then the elbow, then the hanky, then the tissue. Which stops the most drops? Look at the hand afterwards too.
flow.kid: Try each cover. Spray once. Measure. Which stops most? Look at the hand. Is it wet?
flow.parent: Most covers stop most drops. The point is what happens next: the hand is wet with coloured water, and would spread germs to whatever it touches. The elbow and the tissue keep the drops off hands. Use fresh newspaper, or move along, for each test.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and creative ideas. Then invent your own.
flow.say: The hand stopped the drops, but now it's wet. What would that hand touch next?
flow.kid: The hand caught the drops. But now it is wet! What would it touch next? Invent your own catcher.

check.q: Why is sneezing into your elbow better than into your hand?
options: Your hand would then spread germs to everything you touch, but you rarely touch things with your elbow
Elbows have no germs
Hands are too small to catch a sneeze
check.why: Both can catch drops. But hands go on to touch door handles, food and faces. Elbows don't. Picking 'elbows have no germs' is not right. It is about where the germs go next.

challenges.context: This is a test-and-design challenge. You use a spray bottle as a pretend sneeze to find the best way to catch sneezes.

challenges.title: Soap for Everyone
challenges.problem: At a wedding or a school, lots of people wash their hands at one tap. The soap gets lost, dropped on the floor, or used up. Design a way to keep soap clean, easy to reach and shared by many people.
constraints: A small child must be able to reach and use it.
The soap must not sit in a puddle, because wet soap goes soft and slimy.
materials: an old bar of soap, string, an old net bag or a stocking, a plastic bottle, and a nail used by a grown-up
general: Soap on a string, tied beside the tap.
A soap dish with holes, so the water drains away.
Liquid soap in a pump bottle.
creative: Make 'soapy water' by dissolving soap scraps in a bottle of water with a hole in the cap. It can't be lost and is shared easily.
Put soap in an old stocking or onion net, tied to the tap. The net also helps you scrub.
Use reetha water in a bottle, as people did before soap bars.

check.q: Why is soap that hangs or drains better than soap in a puddle?

opts: A tiny living thing or virus that can make us ill
quiz.why: Germs are the microbes and viruses that can make us ill. Picking 'every microbe' misses that most microbes are harmless or helpful. Picking 'insect' mixes germs with the pests that can carry them.

quiz.p: How do germs most often get into our bodies?
opts: Hands carry them to our eyes, nose and mouth
They grow out of our hair
quiz.why: Hands carry germs to the soft, wet linings of the eyes, nose and mouth. Picking 'through dry skin' misses that skin is a strong wall, unless there is a cut.

quiz.p: Why does water alone leave most germs on your hands?
opts: Germs stick in the skin's oil, and water slides off oil
quiz.why: Water molecules hold on to each other, not to oil. So water runs over the oily layer where germs stick. Picking 'too cold' is common, but warm and cold water work about the same.

opts: A water-loving head and an oil-loving tail
quiz.why: Its two different ends let it hold oil and water both, so water can carry oil and germs away. Picking 'tiny teeth' imagines soap as a fighter. It works more like a carrier.

quiz.p: In the jar test, why did the soapy jar stay cloudy?
opts: Soap wrapped tiny oil drops so they stayed mixed in water
quiz.why: Each oil drop is wrapped in soap molecules, tails in and heads out. Picking 'disappear' misses that the oil is still there, just in tiny wrapped drops.
quiz.context: In the jar test, you shake oil and water in two jars and add soap to only one.

quiz.p: In the haldi test, which wash left the least yellow?
opts: Soap for 20 seconds, rubbing every part
quiz.why: Soap plus 20 seconds of rubbing reaches all the oil, even between fingers. Picking soap for 5 seconds usually means thinking soap works instantly.
quiz.context: In the haldi test, you coat your hands with oil and haldi as pretend germs, then wash three different ways.

chart.title: Made-up example: yellow left after washing, from 0 (none) to 5 (all)

quiz.p: When is it MOST important to wash your hands with soap?
opts: Before eating and after the toilet
quiz.why: Those are the moments germs most easily travel to your mouth, or from waste to other people. Picking 'after reading' is a kind thought, but books rarely carry germs that make us ill.

quiz.p: Which is the safe way to care for your ears?
opts: Wipe the outer ear, and never poke anything inside
quiz.why: Earwax cleans itself out. Poking can hurt the eardrum. Picking a hairpin is a common, risky habit.

opts: Kept clean and private, and your body belongs to you
Something you can never talk about with anyone
Not really part of your body
quiz.why: They are part of you, kept clean and private. You can always talk to a trusted grown-up about them, especially if any touch feels wrong. Picking 'never talk about' is what makes children unsafe, so it is not right.

quiz.p: Why do we empty pots, trays and coolers of still water once a week?
opts: Mosquito eggs in them become flying mosquitoes in about a week
quiz.why: Emptying the water before the young mosquitoes grow up stops them. Picking 'smells' echoes the old bad-air idea. The problem is the mosquitoes, not the smell.
quiz.context: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water, even in a flowerpot tray.

quiz.p: Which of these protects a whole town from germs?
opts: Clean water, toilets and covered drains
quiz.why: Clean water and sanitation stop germs reaching many people at once. Picking 'hospital only' misses that hospitals mostly treat illness after it starts.

opts: Made doctors wash their hands in chlorine water before touching mothers
quiz.why: The washing basin made deaths in his ward fall sharply. Picking 'microscope' is a mix-up: microscopes were around for 200 years before him.

quiz.p: Semmelweis compared his ward with another, safer ward. Who ran it?
quiz.why: The midwives' ward had far fewer fevers. Their careful work gave Semmelweis his clue. Picking another answer usually means the midwives were left out of the story, as they often are.
Only a small number of microbes are germs. Many help us, the soil and the sea. Picking 'germs' is a very common belief, often from adverts.

quiz.p: What do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether too few harmless microbes in early life helps cause allergies
quiz.why: The hygiene hypothesis and the 'old friends' idea are still debated. Picking the others misses that germs and soap are well understood.

applications: Hand-washing in homes, schools and hospitals stops tummy bugs, colds and flu spreading.
Doctors and nurses scrub before surgery, and boil or heat their tools to kill germs.
Boiling, filtering and treating drinking water stops cholera, typhoid and other illnesses.
Toilets, sewers and drains keep waste away from water and food.
Covering food and water keeps flies and dust off.
Emptying still water every week stops mosquitoes that carry dengue and malaria.
Dishwashing liquid, shampoo and laundry soap all use two-ended molecules like soap.
Reetha and shikakai are still used to wash hair, silk and jewellery in India.
Food factories and restaurants follow hygiene rules to keep food safe.
Microbes are used to make curd, idli, dosa, bread and cheese.
Doctors are testing bacteriophages, viruses that kill bacteria, as medicines for germs that antibiotics can no longer kill.
Global Handwashing Day, every 15 October, reminds the world that soap saves lives.

open_questions.q: How much contact with harmless microbes do children need to stay healthy?
open_questions.why_open: Studies of farm children suggest it matters, but nobody knows which microbes, how much, or when.

open_questions.q: Why do our skins carry the particular microbes they do?
open_questions.why_open: Each person's skin has a different mix, and it changes with age, place and season. Scientists are still mapping it.

open_questions.q: Was Hankin seeing bacteriophages in Ganga water in 1896?
open_questions.why_open: It seems very likely, but his water samples are gone, so nobody can check.

open_questions.q: Can bacteriophages replace antibiotics for some illnesses?
open_questions.why_open: Some patients have been helped, but large careful tests are still going on.

open_questions.q: Do cleaning chemicals that kill germs help germs become resistant?
open_questions.why_open: Some laboratory studies suggest they might. How much it happens in real homes is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How did the very first cells get their walls?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think soap-like molecules folded into bubbles in water, billions of years ago. Laboratories are testing the idea, but nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Why do people touch their faces so often?
open_questions.why_open: It may help us calm down or think, but scientists do not fully know.

maths.problem: In the face-touch count, your grown-up touched their face 4 times in 10 minutes. There are 6 lots of 10 minutes in an hour. About how many face touches is that in one hour?
maths.answer: About 24 face touches in one hour.
maths.explain: 4 touches every 10 minutes. An hour has 6 lots of 10 minutes. 4 × 6 = 24. So about 24 touches in an hour. That is close to what scientists found: about 23 times an hour.
maths.context: In the face-touch count, you secretly count how many times a grown-up touches their face in 10 minutes.
maths.why_maths: We counted for only 10 minutes. Multiplying lets us estimate a whole hour without counting all hour long.

maths.problem: Happy Birthday takes about 10 seconds to sing once. How many times must you sing it to wash your hands for 20 seconds? How many seconds would singing it 3 times take?
maths.answer: 2 times for 20 seconds. Singing it 3 times takes 30 seconds.
maths.explain: Each song is about 10 seconds. 10 + 10 = 20, so 2 songs make 20 seconds. 10 + 10 + 10 = 30, so 3 songs take 30 seconds.
maths.context: In the haldi test, you wash with soap for 20 seconds by singing Happy Birthday while you rub your hands.
maths.why_maths: Counting 20 seconds in your head is hard while you scrub. Knowing how long a song lasts turns the song into a clock.

maths.problem: Look at the chart of yellow left after washing. Water only scored 4. Soap for 20 seconds scored 0. Soap for 5 seconds scored 2. Put the three ways in order from cleanest to least clean. How many points cleaner was soap for 20 seconds than water only?
maths.answer: Cleanest to least clean: soap 20 seconds, soap 5 seconds, water only. Soap for 20 seconds was 4 points cleaner.
maths.explain: A lower score means less yellow left. 0 is lowest, then 2, then 4. So the order is soap 20 seconds, soap 5 seconds, water only. 4 take away 0 is 4, so it was 4 points cleaner.
maths.context: In the haldi test, you score how much yellow is left after washing, from 0 for none to 5 for all.

chart.title: Made-up example: yellow left after washing, from 0 (none) to 5 (all)

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows the cleanest wash at a glance. Here the shortest bar wins, which is a good thing to notice.

maths.problem: You filled your tippy-tap bottle with 1,500 millilitres of water. It gave 30 hand-washes before it was empty. How much water did one wash use?
maths.explain: Share 1,500 millilitres equally between 30 washes. 1,500 ÷ 30 is the same as 150 ÷ 3, which is 50. You can check: 30 × 50 = 1,500. 50 millilitres is about a quarter of a small steel tumbler.
maths.context: In the tippy-tap project, you build a hand-washing station from a 2-litre bottle filled three-quarters full, and count how many washes it gives.
maths.why_maths: Dividing tells us how little water each wash really needs. That matters in places where every bucket is carried from far away.

maths.problem: In the bread test, on day 7 you counted the mould spots. Not touched: 1. Dirty hands: 9. Water only: 5. Soap: 2. Make a tally chart, then answer: how many more spots did the dirty hands slice have than the soap slice?
maths.explain: Draw tally marks for each slice: 1, 9, 5 and 2. The dirty hands slice had 9 spots. The soap slice had 2. 9 take away 2 is 7. So the dirty hands slice had 7 more spots.
maths.context: In the bread test, you touch slices of bread with hands cleaned in different ways, then count spots of mould after a week.

roots.context: We have been learning how soap, water and clean habits keep germs away. Now we ask what being clean tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Clean does not mean empty of life. It means the right life in the right place.
deep_truth.habit: We sort the world into clean and dirty, and microbes into enemies. But your skin is home to millions of friendly microbes, and soil is lovely in a garden but not on a plate. Dirt is not a kind of thing. It is something in the wrong place.
deep_truth.evidence: Soap washes away the visitor microbes from things you touch, but your resident skin microbes stay. And soap breaks a virus's coat only because that coat is built from the same kind of molecules as your own cells.

three.who_am_i: You are not only you. Millions of microbes live on your skin, and your cell walls are built like soap.
three.what_is_life: Life is always moving from one place to another, on hands, in water and through the air.
three.what_is_this_world: A world where cats, crows, bees and people all keep clean, each in their own way, for their own reasons.

roots.thread: A soap molecule is one thing with two sides. One side loves water, the other loves oil, and because it holds both, it can bring them together. Your cells are wrapped in the same kind of two-sided molecule. So are the coats of some viruses. The microbes on your skin and the cells of your body share one home. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as many: soap, cell, microbe and child are made of the same stuff, arranged in different ways. Hygiene is not a war against life. It is caring for where each part of it belongs.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son to put salt in water overnight. In the morning the salt cannot be seen, but every sip tastes salty. What is unseen can still be everywhere.
teachings.link: Germs and soap molecules are far too small to see. Like the salt, we know they are there by what they do: mould on bread, a fever in a ward, pepper rushing to the edge of a plate.

teachings.teaching: Among the five personal practices, the niyamas, the first is shaucha: cleanliness of the body and clarity of the mind.
teachings.link: In this teaching, washing is not only about germs. It is also a way of paying attention, of beginning again, fresh.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988), on interbeing
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain, the tree and the logger in it. Everything is made of things that are not itself.
teachings.link: Look deeply at your hand and you find skin, oil, water and millions of microbes. You are made of many lives that are not only 'you'.

science.text: Every cell is wrapped in a membrane of molecules with water-loving heads and oil-loving tails, built much like soap.
About as many bacteria live on and in a person as there are human cells in their body.
The first cells may have begun when soap-like molecules folded into tiny bubbles in water, billions of years ago.

other_view.view: Some germs kill, and treating them as enemies has saved millions of lives. The microbes on our skin are simply living where there is food and space. That is chemistry and evolution, not oneness. This is an honest view, and the science in it is true.

Where is that water going now? Who will it meet next?
